projectOutComesReport:
The project Collaborative Research: Algebra Instruction at Community Colleges: Validating Measures of Quality Instruction (VMQI) represents a comprehensive effort to investigate and improve mathematics education in the community college sector. Historically a neglected area of research, community college algebra serves as a critical “gateway" course for students pursuing STEM majors. Led by a team of collaborators, practitioners and researchers at community college and at four-year institutions in four states, the project aimed to define and validate the mathematical knowledge required for teaching (MKT) at this level, identify characteristics of high-quality instruction, and explore the connection between teacher knowledge and instructional quality.

The project was structured around three research questions:

1.    RQ1: Identifying the dimensions of mathematical knowledge for teaching college algebra specifically within community colleges.

2.    RQ2: Examining the relationship between high-quality instruction and the classroom environment as described by the students’ sense of belonging? 

3.    RQ3: Investigating the link between an instructor's MKT and the observed quality of their algebra instruction.

To address these questions, the research team developed and validated two major instruments: the Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching Community College Algebra (MKT-CCA) instrument and the Evaluating the Quality of Instruction in Postsecondary Mathematics (EQIPM) tool.

Significant Findings and Results

A major outcome of the project was the validation of the MKT-CCA instrument. Although the instrument was designed with a six-dimensional blueprint in mind (three topics: Linear, Rational, and Exponential Functions; and two tasks of teaching: Choosing problems and Understanding Student Work), psychometric modeling confirmed that a one-dimensional model provided the best fit for the data. The instrument is sensitive to knowledge changes in graduate student populations and indicates that an instructor’s MKT, combined with the reported frequency of tasks of teaching, influences their beliefs about their own teaching practice. This suggests that targeted professional development can positively alter how mathematics faculty perceive their work with community college students.

The team faced challenges in operationalizing students’ classroom sense of belonging for augmenting the EQIPM instrument (RQ2). Not only was it difficult to capture complex belonging behavior related to high-quality instruction with a single-lesson video segment, but such approach did not consider other resources that are necessary for empowering students. Using Q-Sort methodology, the team identified distinct groups of students who shared similar classroom experiences and beliefs. A key finding was that students generally felt a higher sense of belonging to "mathematics" as a discipline than to their specific instructors or peers, with peer belonging scores typically being the lowest.

In exploring the connection between knowledge and instruction (RQ3), case studies of instructors provided evidence that the project’s instruments, including a measure of students’ knowledge, are sensitive to the specialized knowledge needed for instruction that impacts student learning. The analysis confirmed two distinct dimensions of instructional quality: Instructor-Content Interaction and Instructor-Student Interaction.

The project served as a robust training ground for a diverse team of researchers. Post-doctoral fellows gained expertise in project management, instrument design, and mentoring. Graduate students developed skills in qualitative analysis using tools like Dedoose, protocol design, data collection and management, and psychometrics. Undergraduate students learned data management, item piloting, and participated in dissemination efforts. Additionally, the continued involvement of community college faculty as research associates built long-term capacity for independent research.

The VMQI project has had a significant impact on the discipline of mathematics education (intellectual merit) and the broader STEM pipeline (broader impact)

  • Disciplinary Advancement: By providing validated instruments like MKT-CCA and EQIPM, the project offers researchers reliable tools to evaluate the efficacy of professional development interventions. It also established the viability of Q-Sort methodology for studying student experiences.

  • Impact on Other STEM Fields: The research techniques and findings regarding student belonging are directly applicable to other STEM integrated courses, particularly those at community colleges with highly diverse student populations.

  • Strengthening the STEM Pipeline: College algebra is a high-stakes course that determines student persistence in STEM. By identifying the specific instructional qualities that foster student growth and conceptual understanding, this research helps ensure that a more diverse range of students can successfully transition into STEM careers.

  • Societal Contribution: The project validates the professional expertise of community college faculty and provides them with data-driven tools to improve their practice. Through extensive dissemination at national and international conferences, these findings reach practitioners globally, aiming to improve the educational outcomes and economic mobility of millions of community college students.

The project’s focus on the community college sector—a historically neglected area of instructional research—validates the professional expertise of community college faculty. The dissemination of these findings through numerous national and international conferences (such as JMM, MathFest, AMATYC, RUME, PME, ICME, AfriCME, and many regional conferences from AMATYC and the MAA) speaks of the project’s efforts to reach practitioners aiming to improve the educational outcomes and economic mobility of community college students.

This project will contribute to the national need for well-educated scientists, mathematicians, engineers, and technicians by supporting the retention and graduation of high-achieving, low-income students with demonstrated financial need at Augsburg University, Century College, Minneapolis College, and Normandale Community College. These undergraduate institutions serve populations that are 48-67% Pell-eligible and 40-62% students of color. Over 5 years, this project will fund scholarships and provide research opportunities for 195 unique full-time and part-time students who are pursuing bachelor’s degrees in Biology, Chemistry, Computer Science, Engineering, Food Science, Mathematics, and Physics. The project will recruit, retain, and support three 2-year scholar cohorts at the three community colleges who will enter a Minnesota STEM Transfer pathway leading to admission to a baccalaureate STEM program. The project will also recruit, retain, and support a 4-year scholar cohort at Augsburg University beginning at the start of upper-level STEM coursework leading to degree completion and transition to the STEM workforce or graduate education. This project builds on successful strategies for achieving early exposure to undergraduate research and internship experiences for students and supporting student professional development through cross-institutional partnerships, as well as partnership with workforce development programs.

The overall goal of this project is to increase recruitment, retention, transfer, student success, graduation, and entry to the STEM workforce of low-income, high-achieving undergraduate STEM scholars with demonstrated financial need. The project builds on established theories regarding the importance and value of mentoring and other high impact practices (HIPs) such as involvement in undergraduate research and internships. It also recognizes that there is great talent and potential among students who begin their academic careers at community colleges. Scholars will be connected to internships and research experiences through SciTech, UpTurnships, MnDRIVE, and Augsburg University’s undergraduate research programs. Professional development for faculty mentors and assessment from the Center for the Improvement of Mentored Experiences in Research (CIMER) will provide data to develop new knowledge about how institutional and cross-institutional factors affect students and mentors across different social identities. Knowledge generation and evaluation utilizes the CIMER Assessment Platform, the Cultural Intelligence Scale, HIP quality and equity measures, and other institutional metrics for tracking transfers. This project is funded by NSF’s Scholarships in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics program, which seeks to increase the number of low-income academically talented students with demonstrated financial need who earn degrees in STEM fields. It also aims to improve the education of future STEM workers, and to generate knowledge about academic success, retention, transfer, graduation, and academic/career pathways of low-income students.

projectOutComesReport:
This Collaborative Research award focused on generating knowledge about how cross-institution scholarship partnerships can strengthen the professional preparation of STEM students with financial need in Minnesota. The work was conducted through the PRISM consortium, which brought together Augsburg University, Century College, Minneapolis College, and Normandale Community College. A research partnership housed at the University of Minnesota coordinated the multi-site study to better understand what helps students persist and succeed in STEM.

The project developed a shared research and evaluation framework across institutions to examine how participation in PRISM supports students’ academic, social, and emotional development; how program structures shape mentors’ practices and students’ experiences across institutional contexts; and how the partnership is implemented and sustained in practice. The team used a coordinated, multi-site design that combined institutional outcome data (course completion, GPA, persistence, and transfer indicators) with repeated student surveys and qualitative assessments to explore patterns in students' experiences over time.

The team conducted a rigorous program evaluation using propensity score matching techniques to compare PRISM scholars with similar non-participants who met eligibility criteria. This approach reduced the risk of self-selection bias and strengthened evidence about program impacts. Published results showed that PRISM scholars earned higher cumulative and STEM GPAs, completed more STEM courses, and were much less likely to withdraw (5.9% vs. 28.4%) than comparable non-scholars.

The project also generated longitudinal, multi-campus survey data to better understand the student experience behind those outcomes. Annual surveys were distributed across all partner institutions and measured academic and psychosocial factors tied to STEM persistence, including STEM identity, self-efficacy, mentoring quality, engagement in high-impact practices, cultural identity, and mental health. These data supported descriptive and comparative analyses over time (for example, changes in STEM achievement indicators and mentorship experiences), helping the program identify strengths and areas needing attention, such as belonging and well-being, so that supports could be targeted. 

A second line of knowledge generation used mixed methods to connect students’ narratives to STEM persistence. A published study examined STEM-related autobiographical memories and linked narrative features (such as specificity, context, and meaning-making) with science identity and academic outcomes (including STEM grades and number of STEM courses taken). Findings suggest that how students interpret formative STEM experiences may be associated with identity development and continued engagement in STEM coursework.

In the final year, the team completed a collaborative autoethnography in which PRISM program leaders served as both participants and co-researchers, using collective reflection to surface the “how” and “why” behind key program decisions and partnership practices. Data were generated through structured, recorded, and transcribed sessions (with iterative written reflections) and analyzed using thematic analysis. This method strengthens the field by making partnership implementation visible and analyzable, specifically by capturing insider perspectives on coordination, relationship-building, and day-to-day decision-making that metrics may not adequately document, and by translating those insights into practical strategies that other multi-institution STEM pathway and scholarship initiatives can adapt and implement. 

The project demonstrated that a coordinated, cross-institution scholarship partnership is associated with stronger academic progress among participating STEM students. It clarified the mechanisms that support this progress, including mentoring, structured developmental experiences, and the coordination required to implement a multi-campus program effectively. By integrating institutional outcome tracking with longitudinal student surveys, qualitative inquiry, and an implementation-focused collaborative autoethnography, the project produced evidence and transferable insights that can inform how other colleges and universities design, strengthen, and sustain STEM pathway partnerships.

abstractText:
The minerals that comprise Earth’s crust and mantle undergo phase transformations. Changes in their crystal structure occur in response to changes in temperature and pressure. With increasing pressure, olivine — the main constituent of the upper mantle  — transforms into denser minerals; much like graphite transforms into diamond. As one mineral transforms into another, crystal defects, known as dislocations, are produced. Dislocations allow crystals to deform plastically, i.e., permanently.  These dislocations can cause temporary weakening that speeds up crust and mantle flows. Transformation-induced weakening  — "transformation plasticity"  —  may impact the mantle flows driving plate tectonics. It may also provide an explanation for the earthquakes occurring at great depths in the mantle.  These deep earthquakes are still poorly understood. Despite its importance, transformation plasticity has seldom been observed in the laboratory. This is because it involves complex processes, difficult to quantify by conventional methods. Here, The researchers  conduct experiments at the extreme pressures and temperature prevailing in the mantle.  They study the plasticity of fayalite, olivine Fe-rich end member, and quartz which is an important constituent of the continental crust. They use a state-of-the-art high-pressure deformation device set up at a national synchrotron facility.  There, powerful X-rays allow imaging the minerals and analyzing their properties during their transformations.  The multidisciplinary project, at the intersection of geophysics, materials science, and crystallography, aims to expand the understanding of Earth’s interior dynamics. It supports the professional development of an early career scientist. It also provides training for one graduate and several undergraduate students.

Transformation plasticity may play a central role in: 1) mantle decoupling and the development of layered convection; 2) slab ponding in Earth’s mantle transition zone; 3) shear zone nucleation during orogenesis; 4) mantle plume upwelling; and 5) the nucleation of deep-focus earthquakes. However, few studies have examined transformation plasticity in major rock-forming minerals. This is because of the difficulty to quantify complex transient behaviors at high temperatures (>1000 K) and pressures (> 1 GPa). Here, the team explores the quartz-coesite and olivine-spinel phase transformations  — under hydrostatic and non-hydrostatic conditions  — using a Deformation-DIA (D-DIA) apparatus located at the Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Laboratory. This experimental setup is uniquely suited to examining transformation-related phenomena in situ at mantle pressures and temperatures. Stresses and transformation kinetics are quantified via energy-dispersive X-ray diffraction. Axial and volume strains are measured using X-ray radiography. Constitutive laws describing transformation plasticity are derived, benchmarked against experimental data, and extrapolated to Earth conditions. Run product microstructures are also investigated in detail — using high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction — to interrogate the physical processes responsible for transformation-induced weakening. Ultimately, the team seeks to determine the importance of transformation plasticity in Earth’s crust and mantle.

program: STUDIES OF THE EARTH'S DEEP INTERIOR
projectOutComesReport:
Researchers have long recognized that rocks can deform more easily as their constituent minerals undergo phase transformations—that is, abrupt changes in crystal structure at elevated pressures and temperatures. Examples include the transformation of graphite to diamond, quartz to coesite, and olivine (peridot) to spinel, to name just a few. Such weakening is thought to strongly influence the transport of rocks during subduction, mantle convection, and continental collision and mountain building. Unfortunately, transformation-induced weakening has thus far proven remarkably difficult to study in the laboratory, given the technical difficulties of directly observing rocks and minerals at the high-pressure, high-temperature conditions required to produce most geologically relevant phase transitions.


In this project, we overcame these technical challenges by performing experiments at a particle accelerator facility, the Advanced Photon Source synchrotron (Argonne National Laboratory, Chicago, IL). Using high-powered X-rays, we were able to directly witness the transformation of quartz to coesite (SiO2) and olivine to spinel (Fe2SiO4) at pressures of up to 1 million psi and temperatures of up to 1000°C. We found that these phase transformations did indeed produce dramatic weakening, which, when extrapolated to natural conditions, is consistent with the stagnation (buckling) of oceanic crust being subducted underneath the western Pacific. Meanwhile, we have begun examining our experimental specimens using state-of-the-art electron microscope techniques. We find elevated concentrations of crystal defects in SiO2 and Fe2SiO4 specimens extracted mid-way through their respective phase transformations, which explain the observed weakening. Finally, we have developed new tools for identifying rocks that have previously undergone phase transformations before being exhumed to Earth’s surface. Together, these outcomes mark a major step forward in understanding the dynamic feedbacks among metamorphism and rock deformation. Such work will enable researchers to build a more complete picture of Earth’s dynamic history and, through, numerical simulations, future evolution.


This project supported the professional development of one first-time principal investigator, one postdoctoral investigator, and numerous students who accompanied our team to the Advanced Photon Source facility as part of a shadowing program.

abstractText:
The ERC for Advanced Technologies for the Preservation of Biological Systems (ATP-Bio) aims to “stop biological time” and radically extend the ability to bank and transport cells, aquatic embryos, tissue, skin, whole organs, microphysiological systems (“organs-on-a-chip”), and even whole organisms through a team approach to build advanced biopreservation technologies. In order to build a more robust STEM workforce, especially in the growing number of fields needing biopreservation technologies, ATP-Bio aims for STEM education across all components of the Center. As such, ATP-Bio’s workforce development plan is purposefully designed to promote interest and engagement in STEM for all students. ATP-Bio will engage middle schoolers and high schoolers with biopreservation science and technology, fund numerous research internships in ATP-Bio labs for undergraduates, sponsor dozens of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in ATP-Bio labs and facilitate dozens of internships in the biopreservation industry. ATP-Bio will also include a focused effort on Ethics and Public Policy so that the Center’s technology will be legally and ethically translated to public benefit. Together with a large and active group of industrial partners, ATP-Bio aims to produce massive social benefit through “off-the-shelf” biopreservation technologies for cell therapies, tissue and organ transplantation, pharmacological research, aquaculture, agriculture and many other fields.

ATP-Bio will accomplish its goals by engineering technologies for biological systems before cooling, during cooling and stasis at subzero temperatures, and during rewarming to normal biological temperatures. At each stage, ATP-Bio convergent science teams will aim to eliminate or control ice formation, mitigate the toxicity of cryopreservation agents, and eliminate thermal and mechanical stress. Engineering and Workforce Development activities across all components of ATP-Bio is aimed at creating a STEM workforce that understands team science, especially for the growing number of fields needing biopreservation technologies. ATP-Bio will leverage the long-term nature of an ERC to conduct research on developing positive STEM identity for all students and improving STEM pathways for K-12 and undergraduate STEM education. ATP-Bio will also include focused research on Ethics and Public Policy so that the Center’s technology will be legally and ethically translated to public benefit.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
Understanding the flow and transport of particles (e.g., snow, sand, pollens, etc.) in atmospheric environments is critical for applications related to wind energy, meteorology (e.g., snow settling), geomorphology (e.g., desert migration), oceanography (e.g., spray generation), agriculture (e.g., pollen dispersal), public health (e.g., airborne disease transmission), etc. These processes involve flows over a broad range of spatial and temporal scales and complex atmospheric phenomena which are impossible to be fully reproduced in the laboratory. Conventional field measurements (e.g. meteorological tower, LiDAR, Sodar and Radar) of these processes do not have sufficient resolutions to probe into their detailed underlying physics. To bridge this gap, with a team of flow physicists, computer scientists, and engineers, the proposal aims to develop a Grand-scale Atmospheric Imaging Apparatus (GAIA), a stand-alone and imaging-based field measuring system, able to quantify atmospheric flows and particle transport over large sample regions with unprecedented spatiotemporal resolution. Though collaboration with 11 university, national labs and industries across the globe, GAIA will enable fundamental and applied research across engineering, geoscience and computer science, and will support a number of existing educational programs involving underrepresented groups and minorities. 

The goal of the project is to develop a Grand-scale Atmospheric Imaging Apparatus (GAIA),   envisioned as a field instrument conducting particle image/tracking velocimetry (PIV/PTV) by exploiting particles (e.g., snow, sand, pollen, droplets, etc.) naturally present in the atmosphere to investigate both flow (using them as tracers) and the transport of the particles themselves depending on their inertial properties with respect to the flow. The development of GAIA innovates every single component of conventional PIV/PTV including both the hardware and processing software to address key challenges in conducting high-resolution flow imaging under harsh field conditions. Specifically, GAIA involves multi-mode and multi configuration Lego design and mechanical automation for the hardware and an integration of PIV/PTV concept with state-of-the-art machine learning multiview 3D scene reconstruction for data processing. Such innovation enables GAIA to conduct high-resolution imaging of flow and particle transport across a broad range of scales with sample volumes up to orders of magnitude larger than those of conventional PIV/PTVs. In addition, GAIA incorporates several unique sensors (e.g., digital inline holography) for in situ characterization of meteorological conditions and particle properties (e.g. shape, concentration, etc.) with unprecedented details. The GAIA will be tested under different field conditions in conjunction with cutting-edge 3D Doppler scanning LiDARs. Such integration enables the first-ever measurements of atmospheric flow and particle transport from sub-meter to kilometer scales, providing benchmark datasets not only for the fundamental study of atmospheric flow and particle transport, but also for learning-based motion reconstruction in computer science.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
Fungi play an essential role in forest ecosystems, breaking down leaf litter and woody debris that has fallen to the forest floor.  As this organic matter is decomposed by fungi, much of it is incorporated into soils, adding to the significant carbon and nitrogen pools they harbor. There is growing recognition that ectomycorrhizal fungi, which form nutritional symbioses with many forest trees, can slow the breakdown of organic matter and stabilize soil carbon. This research seeks to critically assess how ectomycorrhizal fungal suppress organic matter decomposition, and to characterize the impacts of this suppression on soil carbon and nitrogen dynamics. Determining how ectomycorrhizal fungi mediate carbon and nutrient fluxes during the decomposition of organic matter will be useful for forest management focused on carbon retention in soils and on tree health. In addition, defining the scope of ectomycorrhizal fungal suppression of organic matter decomposition across diverse temperature and moisture conditions will be important for accurately formulating carbon and nitrogen dynamics in Earth system models. This project provides support for science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) graduate and undergraduate mentoring, K-12 experiential learning, and public engagement through collaborations with the Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Reserve, Minute Earth, California Academy of Sciences, and the Florida Museum of Natural History. 

The capacity of ectomycorrhizal fungi to modify organic matter decomposition is hypothesized to depend on three factors: organic matter chemistry, ectomycorrhizal fungal community composition, and environmental conditions. This hypothesis will be tested with a series of field-based experiments at research sites in Minnesota, Florida, and California. By utilizing a single research site in Minnesota in which a wide range of organic matter types are concurrently deployed across forest stands differing in ectomycorrhizal fungal community composition, the independent and interactive roles of organic matter chemistry and ectomycorrhizal fungal community composition can be determined while holding multiple environmental variables constant. At the same time, by deploying a common organic matter type across multiple sites varying in temperature and precipitation (in Minnesota, Florida, and California), the extent to which variation in edaphic conditions influence ectomycorrhizal fungal suppression of organic decomposition can also be assessed. Additionally, detailed analyses of the carbon held in various soil fractions will provide a critical missing link between ectomycorrhizal fungal-induced changes in organic matter decomposition rates and retention of carbon in soil.

projectOutComesReport:
Forests play a central role in regulating Earth’s climate because they store large amounts of carbon in soils and recycle nutrients that sustain plant growth. A major driver of these processes is the decomposition of organic matter, including fallen leaves, roots, wood, and dead fungal tissue. This collaborative research project examined how interactions among different groups of fungi, especially ectomycorrhizal fungi that live in close partnership with trees, influence how quickly organic matter decomposes and how long carbon remains stored in forest soils.

Ectomycorrhizal fungi help trees acquire nutrients such as nitrogen in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis. For decades, ecologists have hypothesized that these fungi can slow decomposition by competing with free-living decomposer fungi for nutrients, a phenomenon often called the Gadgil effect. While widely discussed and cited, the scope and long-term consequences of this effect across different forest types, soil depths, and organic matter sources remained poorly understood. A central goal of this project was to directly test when and where ectomycorrhizal fungi influence decomposition and soil carbon storage.

Over the life of the award, we conducted coordinated field experiments, laboratory incubations, and molecular analyses across multiple forest sites. These studies showed that ectomycorrhizal fungi do influence decomposition, but not in a single or universal way. In some forest soils, reducing ectomycorrhizal fungal activity increased decomposition and led to measurable losses of soil carbon, particularly in surface soils and relatively fast-cycling organic matter pools. In other contexts, including comparisons across broader environmental gradients, ectomycorrhizal fungi had weak or even opposite effects on leaf litter decomposition. Together, these results demonstrate that fungal control over decomposition is strongly context dependent and shaped by soil nutrient availability, organic matter chemistry, soil depth, and fungal community composition.

These findings advance fundamental ecological understanding by showing that decomposition is governed not only by climate and litter quality, but also by biological interactions among microbes belowground. By explicitly linking fungal symbioses to ecosystem-scale carbon storage, this work helps refine ecological theory and improve the representation of soil processes in ecosystem and Earth system models. This is particularly important for predicting forest responses to climate change, where shifts in fungal communities may either enhance or dampen soil carbon loss.

The project also produced broader insights into forest carbon cycling. Complementary work revealed that ectomycorrhizal fungi rely primarily on recently fixed plant carbon, whereas saprotrophic fungi often use much older carbon sources, highlighting fundamental differences in how carbon moves through forest food webs. Additional synthesis efforts showed that decomposition involves a much larger and more dynamic community of microbes than previously recognized.

Multiple broader impacts for this project were achieved. To disseminate findings within the scientific research community, articles were published in diverse ecological journals and presentations made at multiple national and international conferences. To engage the public, the research team contributed to the production of an educational video explaining how fungal interactions influence forest decomposition and carbon storage. This video was released through the widely viewed MinuteEarth YouTube platform, helping make hidden belowground processes accessible to a broad audience. The UMN team also worked with staff at the Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Center to develop a hands-on, multi-year research experience examining how different types of organic material decompose in forest ecosystems. Finally, the project supported the training of multiple PhD students, undergraduate researchers, and a research technician, contributing to workforce development in STEM and preparing trainees for careers in environmental science and research.

This workshop brings together scientists involved in studying atmospheric aerosols at a fundamental level in the laboratory and in the field. The objective of the gathering is to provide molecular level perspectives on aerosol properties that are critical to the impact of aerosols on air quality, climate, and environmental and human health.

The focus will be on the fundamental understanding of atmospheric processes that is needed to interpret and predict climate at both short and long time scales, and on the atmospheric aerosols that are key players that influence these processes. The intellectual merit of this workshop includes the discussion of challenges that exist in understanding the formation of aerosol particles from gaseous precursors and the initial growth of these particles, the internal structure of aerosols, aerosol phase behavior, heterogeneous and multiphase (photo)chemistry, gas-surface interactions, the ability of aerosols to initiate ice and cloud nucleation, the evolution of aerosol optical properties, and the role of bioaerosols in the atmosphere. The workshop will be held at the UCLA Lake Arrowhead Conference Center in September, 2020.  NSF support for this meeting will go towards travel for student, postdoctoral, and early career professionals.

Overview

The proposal provided support for the conference A Molecular-Level Understanding of Atmospheric Aerosols (MUOAA 2022), held at the UCLA Lake Arrowhead Conference Center, May 15-20, 2022 (originally Sept 20-25, 2020; postponed due to COVID-19). This conference gathered 67 scientists involved in studying atmospherically relevant aerosols in the lab, in the field and via advanced modeling techniques. The objective was to provide molecular level perspectives on complex aerosol properties that are critical to the impact of aerosols on air quality, climate and environmental as well as human health.

Intellectual Merit

A fundamental understanding of atmospheric processes is needed to interpret and predict climate at both short and long-time scales, and atmospheric aerosols are key players that influence these processes. Over the past years it has become evident that some barriers to our molecular level understanding of aerosols can only be addressed through fundamental laboratory, theoretical, and modeling studies in chemistry and physics. For example, challenges exist in understanding the formation of aerosol particles from gaseous precursors and the initial growth of these particles, the internal structure of aerosols, aerosol phase behavior, heterogeneous and multiphase (photo)chemistry, gas-surface interactions, the ability of aerosols to initiate ice and cloud nucleation, the evolution of aerosol optical properties, and the role of bioaerosols in the atmosphere. To address these questions, the symposium brought together an international community of researchers interested in all aspects of the molecular chemistry and physics of aerosols.  It provided a unique forum for the participants, who do not normally meet at conferences related to their specific subfield, to exchange ideas on treating these fundamental, complex, and inherently difficult problems.

The conference convened for 4.5 days with a single session track of invited and contributed talks, as well as posters sessions in the evenings. The emphasis was on longer talks, particularly from people new to the MUOAA community, with an integrated discussion at the end of each session that focuses both on the work presented and on the future directions that are critical to the field. The conference had 9 oral presentation sessions and 4 poster sessions.  Each session had built-in discussion time, with discussion leaders leading the discussion with the whole group.  Session topics included:

Aerosol Physical Chemistry: Advanced, emerging, and novel techniques
Aerosol Physical Chemistry: Health and biological aerosols
Aerosol Physical Chemistry: Chemistry and interfaces I, II, III (3 sessions)
Aerosol Physical Chemistry: Ice nucleation
Aerosol Physical Chemistry: New particle formation, clusters, and nanoparticles
Aerosol Physical Chemistry: Water uptake, glassy systems, phase I, II (2 sessions)

Discussion leaders for each session hosted discussions scheduled at the end of each session. Discussion points that crossed over many categories included aerosol pH, defining and understanding surfaces, limits of detections and biases for varied measurement techniques, appropriate model/surrogate chemical systems, and how to incorporate measurements into models. Several hours of unscheduled time were also available for participants throughout the week to engage in further scientific discussion and enhance the opportunity for developing collaborations. Finally, evening poster sessions offered more time for discussion and interactions, and awards were given to the top student posters.    

Broader Impacts

Although the focus of this conference is on atmospherically relevant aerosols, the knowledge exchanged here is directly applicable to industrial processes ranging from the production of pharmaceuticals to maximizing power production in low pressure turbines. The project also provided significant financial support for the travel costs of early career scientists.  Attending the symposium was an enriching experience for all participants, but perhaps particularly for graduate students and post-docs involved in fundamental aerosol research.  The symposium provided a unique opportunity to meet many of the leading, international researchers in the field and to gain exposure to emerging analytical techniques. The significant financial support from the project set aside specifically for travel costs of early career scientists, made it particularly possible for students and post-docs to attend.

abstractText:
With support from the Chemical Measurement & Imaging program, and co-funding from the Interfacial Engineering program, Professor Siepmann and his group at the University of Minnesota-Twin Cities together with collaborators Mark Schure at Kroungold Analytical and Stephanie Schuster at Advanced Materials Technology are investigating processes used to separate the components of chemical mixtures and enable their analysis.  Specifically, they are using advanced simulations to obtain a molecular-level understanding of chromatographic separation processes. “Separation science plays a critical role in maintaining our standard of living and quality of life,” as recently emphasized by the National Academies in a report entitled "A Research Agenda for Transforming Separation Science." Chromatography is an important approach to separations that exploits differences in the interactions of various chemicals with particles packed into a tube (a chromatographic column). Small differences in these interactions get magnified as the mixture passes through the chromatographic column enabling one compound to move more quickly through the column than another and thus, separate. This university-industry team is working to improve understanding of how modifications of the particle surfaces and the use of environmentally benign solvents impact the separation, thereby enabling improved chemical separation systems. This partnership is advancing the education and training of graduate, undergraduate, and high school students, with special efforts made to recruit students from traditionally underrepresented groups in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics.  This effort has relevance to advanced manufacturing as separations is one of the most expensive and time-consuming aspects of the production of industrial scale chemicals.

The underlying principles of liquid and supercritical fluid chromatography are inherently complex, being dictated by the interplay of the sample with the stationary phase (porous solid substrate and bonded ligands) and the mobile phase (often a mixture of solvents). The Siepmann group and Kroungold Analytical are using Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced-sampling algorithms and transferable molecular-mechanics force fields to model and characterize interactions in hydrophilic stationary phases including zwitterionic phases; novel hydrophobic stationary phases with limited flexibility and wettability tuned by the addition of hydrophilic compounds; and supercritical carbon dioxide and hot, compressed water mobile phases. The team is also utilizing coarse-grained models to investigate retention of block copolymers in superficially porous particles. Advanced Materials Technology is leading an effort to carry out synergistic chromatographic measurements. The development of both stationary phases with improved retention characteristics and sustainable mobile phases is being advanced through the molecular-level insights derived from this work.

projectOutComesReport:
Chromatography is one of the principal methods for the analysis and separation of organic and pharmaceutical molecules and of synthetic and biological macromolecules. Chromatography involves a stationary phase that analyte molecules interact with and get retained to different degrees, allowing for separation, and a mobile phase or solvent that transports analytes through the device.  Due to the complexity of chromatographic systems and the lack of atomistic information, however, many fundamental questions on chromatographic retention processes remain unanswered.  Understanding how molecular-level interactions influence separation, i.e., the retention mechanism, is instrumental for improving the performance of existing chromatographic systems and for aiding in the development of future separation technologies.  The collaborative academic-industry research team led by Ilja Siepmann (University of Minnesota), Mark Schure (Kroungold Analytical), and Stephanie Schuster (Advanced Materials Technology) utilized expertise in molecular simulation, synthesis, and characterization to advance knowledge in two focus areas:

Elucidating Structure and Retention in Hydrophilic Liquid Interactions Chromatography (HILIC)

HILIC refers to stationary phases that are water-wettable and permit mobile phases that are high in organic solvent content (e.g., acetonitrile) and with a minor water content; HILIC is advantageous for the separation of complex polar molecules, such as many pharmaceutical compounds. The HILIC stationary phases provide a large fraction of hydroxyl groups or other strong hydrogen bond/donor acceptor moieties (e.g., surface silanols, sSiOH) that interact via hydrogen-bonding with water and analyte molecules. The molecular simulations allow us to separate contributions from the stationary phase and the mobile phase to retention. Non-polar groups are found to interact more favorably with the mobile phase than the stationary phase (i.e., reducing retention), whereas the reverse holds for polar groups. The simulations also reveal that water molecules are enriched at the stationary phase surface, but do not prevent analyte molecules from interacting directly with sSiOH groups (see Image HILIC).

Elucidating Structure and Retention in Supercritical Fluid Chromatography (SFC)

Use of a supercritical-fluid mobile phase increases the speed of analysis and allows for more facile recovery of the solvent, i.e., reducing the environmental burden compared to liquid chromatography. For commonly used stationary phases with long non-polar hydrocarbon chains (e.g., C18 alkyl ligands), we observe that the SFC solvent leads to a swelling of the bonded-chain region with less tilted C18 ligands compared to reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) conditions (see Image SFC). For nonpolar methylene (CH2) segments, the SFC mobile phase is a much stronger solvent than the RPLC mobile phase and, hence, the retention increment of a CH2 group is much smaller in SFC. For a polar hydroxyl (OH) group, the stationary C18 phase at RPLC conditions is more favorable than at SFC conditions because the more significant adsorption of water and methanol for the RPLC system make the stationary phase more polar with a higher concentration of accessible hydrogen-bonding sites for the OH groups of the analytes. Of course, the RPLC solvent provides an even more favorable environment for the OH groups, while the SFC mobile phase is a much weaker solvent. As a consequence, an OH group increases retention in SFC but decreases retention in RPLC.

Research supported by this NSF award afforded, for the first time, a detailed molecular view into retention in HILIC and SFC and into how common stationary phase materials interact with the corresponding mobile phases and are modified by addition of co-solvent (i.e., mobile-phase modifier). These insights are stimulating the thinking for selecting columns and improving stationary phase materials. Chromatographic phases with improved retention characteristics will fill major needs of the chemical, pharmaceutical, and bio-technology industries. Replacing water/organic mobile phases with greener mobile phases will reduce waste and make chromatographic separations more sustainable.

This university-industry partnership has advanced the education and training of two graduate and two undergraduate students by allowing for extensive interactions with industrial researchers and experiences with real-world applications. In addition, a high school student participated remotely during summer 2021. Three of these five junior researchers belong to groups underrepresented in the STEM fields.

This award will partially support the November 2020 and November 2021 Field of Dreams Conferences, to be held on the University of Minnesota campus. The Field of Dreams Conference is organized by the Math Alliance, an organization whose goal is to increase the number of students from backgrounds underrepresented in the mathematical sciences who earn doctorates in those fields, and the Institute for Mathematics and its Applications. Approximately 200 undergraduate and terminal MS students will attend the conference, and about 80% of those will be underrepresented minorities. All funds from this award will be used to pay the cost of attendance for some of these students. The conference coordinates with the Math Alliance's Facilitated Graduate Admissions Process (F-GAP), which has helped place an average of about 80 Math Alliance Scholars per year in graduate programs the last six years with very good retention to this point. The conference is an essential part of a program to produce a more diverse professional mathematical workforce. In addition, there are events at the conference which assist faculty in mentoring practices and help academic departments transform their cultures to be more inclusive and supportive of student success.

The Field of Dreams conference has several purposes, including: providing information about all aspects of the mathematical sciences professions to students wishing to pursue doctoral studies; providing information about summer research programs and opportunities at the NSF-funded Mathematical Sciences Institutes; facilitating appropriate placement of Math Alliance students in graduate programs; providing professional development in mentoring and cultural competence for our Math Alliance faculty; and serving as a clearinghouse for employment opportunities for new (and recent) Math Alliance doctoral recipients. More information about the Math Alliance is available at www.mathalliance.org. Material from previous years' conferences, are available at https://mathalliance.org/field-of-dreams-conference/, and the page for the 2020 conference is https://mathalliance.org/2020-field-of-dreams-conference/.

This grant provided support for the Field of Dreams Conferences held between 2020-2022.  The Field of Dreams is the primary activity of the Math Alliance. The Math Alliance is a community of math sciences faculty and students aimed at

  • increasing the number of doctoral degrees in the mathematical sciences among groups that have been traditionally underrepresented in those fields,
  • improving placement of students from these groups in doctoral programs in disciplines that recruit undergraduate mathematics majors,
  • increasing the number of Ph.D.s from these groups who enter the professoriate in the mathematical sciences as well as other appropriate professions,
  • increasing funded research collaborations among faculty members at the universities with mathematical sciences doctoral programs and faculty members at colleges and universities focused on undergraduate students, and
  • fostering the growth of a community of mathematical scientists that promotes a diverse workforce.

Math Alliance Scholars, who are potential graduate students in the mathematical sciences, participate in programs that have been developed to achieve the above goals. 

Each fall Math Alliance Scholars, together with their Math Alliance Mentors, meet for the Field of Dreams Conference, which typically hosts between 300-500 participants. During the conference, potential graduate students meet with graduate programs in the mathematical sciences as well as professional opportunities in these fields. Scholars spend time with faculty mentors from the Math Alliance schools, get advice on graduate school applications, and attend seminars on graduate school preparation and expectations as well as career seminars. 

This grant provided support during two COVID-impacted years and one in-person conference.  During the two COVID-impacted years, the Field of Dreams was held in a virtual format.

abstractText:
Knowing how to use math and computing skills effectively has become essential to working in science, particularly for biologists in recent years. However, because of the rapid pace of change in biological and computing technologies, many faculty members find themselves teaching skills which are also new to them or that they had to learn independently. In this project, the research team seeks to develop a network of researchers and educators who will collaborate to increase their own computing and statistical skills, while also developing "best practices" of how to teach these skills to students. Using the programming language R, a free and open source coding language that is increasingly used in the biological sciences, the R in Education and Assessment of Learning (REAL) network will establish an inclusive, sustainable community of biology educators and biology education researchers who will both teach and use R for the betterment of biology research and education nationwide. 

The REAL network aims to support the training of biology researchers in quantitative and computational methods; foster collaborations for the development, sharing and assessment of educational modules for quantitative skills and of R-code for biology education researchers; and to catalyze the development of common standards and best practices for the training of undergraduates and graduate students in quantitative and computational skills. The network’s central activity involves training an initial cohort of beginners in R to develop, assess and disseminate biology classroom modules to teach quantitative skills using R and/or develop and test R code scripts and packages tailored specifically for biology education research. REAL trainees will develop novel educational modules to infuse effective, up-to-date quantitative skills into the biology curriculum, rigorously assess the impact of their teaching, and make significant contributions to education research both at the interface of biology and computing and at the edges of current statistical practice. The REAL Network will increase the number of biology faculty with the skills to effectively teach quantitative and computational skills to biology undergraduates, contributing to a new generation of biologists ready to tackle the research and data analysis challenges posed by the development of novel high-throughput technologies. In addition, these faculty will also be better equipped to rigorously assess the educational outcomes of their students, leading to improved teaching practices and allowing for the development of common standards and best practices unique to the training of biologists in quantitative methods.This project is being jointly funded by the Directorate for Biological Sciences, Division of Biological Infrastructure, and the Directorate for Education and Human Resources, Division of Undergraduate Education as part of their efforts to address the challenges posed in Vision and Change in Undergraduate Biology Education: A Call to Action (http://visionandchange/finalreport/).

projectOutComesReport:
The REAL (R in Education and Assessment of Learning) network was established with the primary goal of creating an inclusive network of biology educators who are trained in the programming language R.  The participating educators have been empowered to share their newfound expertise with a new generation of student biologists who, as a result, will be taught in a way that better positions them to tackle the challenges of contemporary and future data collection methods and technologies.  In addition, the newly trained biology faculty learning community participants are in a better position to assess the successes and failures of students within their courses and institutions, which will in turn put them in a better position to steer and drive the adoption of evidence-based best practices in quantitative biology education.

12 participants were selected from a broad pool of over 100 applicants, underscoring the desire within the biology education community for this type of training and community building.  Demographic information provided by participants showed them to represent a diverse cross-section of the biology education community, in terms of race/ethnicity, gender identity, sexual orientation, first-generation status, and institutional affiliation.  The participants participated in an eight week short course in the basics of the R language, which a post-course evaluation indicates led to a significant increase in participant ability and comfort with using R for a range of purposes, including their own research and teaching. Next, participants contributed to two smaller learning communities - one devoted to using R in education research, and the other focused on the production of education materials and curriculum.  The initial results of both learning communities were shared with the broader biology education community at the 2022 Annual Meeting of the Society for the Advancement of Biology Education Research.

abstractText:
Flame spray pyrolysis (FSP) is an advanced technology to synthesize metal oxide powders with a wide range of chemical compositions and physical properties. Because it is readily scalable, FSP has significant applications in powder production for photocatalysts, gas sensors, batteries, solar cells, and fuel cells. While the production of metal oxide nanocrystalline materials has been demonstrated using FSP, it is currently unknown how to control the process to make the chemically pure materials needed for the applications described. Because purely experimental approaches to optimizing the FPS are costly and time-intensive, a new modeling framework for FSP reactors will be developed in this research program to predict how powder particles form and grow in flame reactors. To describe this complex process, the model must integrate elements corresponding to the decomposition chemistry of metal-containing feed components, fuel pyrolysis and oxidation, and aerosol particle nucleation and growth dynamics. The outcome of this combined modeling and experimental program will be a computational tool that can predict the chemical composition, size distribution, and crystal phase of the nanocrystals as the numerous FSP processing parameters are changed. From a fundamental perspective, this project will promote progress in aerosol science and advance the field of chemical reaction engineering. From the application viewpoint, this project will enable computer-based design of FSP reactors capable of high-precision control and significantly reduced fuel costs for nanoparticle manufacturing operations. From an educational perspective, the research team will incorporate the outcomes of this project into their course content, help train the next generation STEM workforce, and continue to include more undergraduates and diversified/under-represented groups into frontier research. 

By leveraging their past success in spray combustion and soot/aerosol modeling, the research team proposes a new modeling framework, with supporting experimental measurements, that will enable model-based design and optimization of FSP reactors for perovskite oxide synthesis. The research project will focus on the synthesis of Lanthanum doped Barium Titanate (La:BaTiO3) by FSP using ethylhexanoate-derived metal precursors and ethylhexanoic acid as a fuel. Experiments to measure the atomic percentages of La, Ba, Ti, and O in mobility-size selected nanocrystals, and the percentages of BaTiO3, BaO, and TiO2 (along with phase information) in the synthesis of La:BaTiO3, will be used to provide validation data for the proposed model. Detailed chemical reaction mechanisms for precursor decomposition, fuel oxidation and pyrolysis, nanoparticle nucleation and surface reactions for multiple metal salt precursors will be identified using a global reaction pathway selection analysis tool developed by the project team. Likewise, a dynamic adaptive chemistry technique will be used as a model reduction method enabling simulations of complex reaction systems using practical levels of computational resources. Finally, a 7-dimensional hybrid sectional-moment model will be developed to track the fractions of BaO, TiO2, and BaTiO3, particle size, and crystallite size specifically to answer whether the nanoparticle composition changes during growth. When complete, the modeling strategy will be broadly applicable to flame pyrolysis systems for a wide range of industrial-scale particle manufacturing applications.

Perovskite oxides (e.g., TiO2) have a broad range of applications in solid oxide fuel cells, as gas sensors, batteries, solar cells, solid oxide fuel cells, and as (photo-)catalysts for a variety of reactions. The development of scalable, rapid, and controllable production/process systems for such materials is hence of great interest for reaction engineering. By leveraging our past successes in soot/aerosol experiment and modeling, we conducted a combined experimental and computational study to understand the TiO2 nanoparticle formation and growth, and to predict the TiO2 nanoparticle size distribution at different conditions.

 

Fundamental studies of nucleation and growth were carried out for the earliest stages of the reaction processes, when the nanoparticles formed are no larger than 3 nm.  We applied a flow tube reactor with a differential mobility analyzer-Faraday cage electrometer system to examine nanocluster formation and growth in the sub-3.0 nm mobility diameter ranges from the decomposition of titanium tetra-isopropoxide (TTIP) in air, for a reactor temperature range of 750 K to 1100 K.  Measurements revealed two types of species in spectra.  First, we detected discrete (narrow) peaks falling in the 0.5 nm to 1.5 nm size range which appear at different locations for positive and negative measurement modes.  Second, we observed a larger, broadly distributed peak, which is similar in intensity for both positive and negative modes after data inversion, and which increases in intensity (concentration) and peak diameter with increasing precursor flow rate, increasing reactor temperature, and increasing residence time.  We concluded that the latter broad peak arises from growing nanoclusters in the reactor.  With regards to the narrower, sub 1.5 nm peaks, the initial discrete peaks, present even in the absence of the organometallic precursor, were attributable to ions formed in the Po-210 bipolar ionization source used to ionize nanoclusters.  However, mobility peaks at new locations emerge when TTIP is introduced and as the reactor temperature is changed; these peaks are mostly likely attributable to specific reactive intermediates from the decomposition of TTIP.  We found that increasing TTIP concentration, reactor temperature, or increasing residence time, which furthers the extent of nanocluster formation, leads to the depletion of the sub 1.5 nm ions.  Because of the large step size in diameter between neighboring sub 1.5 nm peaks, we also found it is unlikely that these peaks arise from TiO2 clusters.  Therefore, our measurements suggested that nanocluster growth from TTIP is facilitated by condensation/surface growth of reactive intermediates from TTIP decomposition, with reactive intermediates detectable via mobility analysis.   Furthermore, while nanocluster formation and growth were clearly detected, measurements did not make clear that the nanoclusters are fully oxidized TiO2 nanoclusters for the synthesis temperature range examined. 

 

The above experimental measurements provided the validation data for the modeling efforts. We developed a sectional method model to track the particle size distribution, with appropriate models developed to describe precursor decomposition and nucleation, condensation/surface growth, and coagulation. The coagulation enhancement factor of nanoparticles is approximately a constant (2.2) at high temperatures of typical flames (>1500 K), but becomes a function of both temperature and particle size at the low temperature range of this study (<1200 K). Specifically, enhancement factor is an exponential decay function of the particle size. We found that enhancement factor can shift the peak in the size distribution of the nanoparticles towards higher diameters if increased, but can also decrease the overall number density due to too extensive coagulation. The modeling framework developed in this project is a very useful tool to enable more rapid development of a synthesis reactor to maximize its performance for the aforementioned emerging applications. In addition, by enabling high performance synthesis, our research outcomes can enable very low fuel consumption during the material processing, and reduce the greenhouse gas emission.

 

From education and training perspective, PIs has incorporated the outcomes of this project into their teaching of undergraduate and graduate courses at the University of Minnesota (UMN), and the course projects provided a good platform for students to obtain hands-on computational and experimental skills. By leveraging the existing REU and UROP programs at UMN, PIs have continued and enlarged their dedication to include more undergraduates and under-represented groups into frontier research. Finally, PI Yang has incorporated the research outcomes from this project to his K-12 STEM outreach workshop at Eureka! program for 8th-12th grade girls (82% of color) from local schools in Summer 2021.

abstractText:
The recent detections of gravitational waves (GWs) from the mergers of binary black hole (BBH) and binary neutron star (BNS) systems have initiated the fields of GW and multi-messenger astrophysics. These discoveries have triggered a broad range of studies including novel tests of General Relativity, constraints on the neutron star equation of state, a new measurement of the Hubble constant H0, and others. Advanced GW detectors are expected to further improve their sensitivities, and to conduct extended observing runs in the next 2-4 years. One of the primary targets of these upcoming runs is the detection of the BBH and BNS gravitational-wave background (SGWB) due to the superposition of all compact binaries in the universe. This project will transform the study of the SGWB by developing new interpretation techniques to combine the GW and electromagnetic (EM) signals and apply them to existing and upcoming data. The project will conduct numerous outreach activities through the Science Museum of Minnesota and will promote involvement of women in astrophysics by connecting with appropriate groups and organizations at the University of Minnesota (UMN).

The main objectives of the project are as follows: 1) Develop techniques for correlating the SGWB directional composition with electromagnetic (EM) tracers of matter structure such as the cosmic microwave background (CMB), the cosmic infrared background (CIB), and galaxy count surveys. 2) Apply the above techniques to the existing and upcoming GW data from aLIGO and aVirgo in correlation with the CMB/CIB data from Planck, and galaxy survey data from SDSS and (upcoming) Euclid. 3) Contribute to the development of the emerging field of multi-messenger astrophysics by establishing new connections between the GW community and the traditional astrophysics community. SGWB-EM correlations will illuminate the origin and the evolution of the compact binaries, potentially resolving the primordial (dark matter) black hole population. They also have the potential to identify and characterize the early universe sources of the SGWB, uncovering the first moments of the universe and probing the physics of very high energies.

orgLongName: Directorate for Mathematical and Physical Sciences
program: Windows on the Universe (WoU)
projectOutComesReport:
Stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) is expected to arise from a superposition of many uncorrelated gravitational wave signals generated throughout the history of the universe. The dominant contribution to this background in the frequency band of terrestrial detectors (Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, Kagra) is expected to come from mergers of binary objects composed of black holes and neutron stars. The background is also expected to be somewhat anisotropic, with spots on the sky featuring higher (or lower) than average gravitational wave energy density. This anisotropy would, therefore, be closely related to the distribution of binary systems across the universe, which in turn depends on the physical processes that led to the formation of such systems. 

The primary goal of this project was to develop techniques for correlating the SGWB directional composition with electromagnetic (EM) tracers of matter structure such as the galaxy count surveys, as well as to develop the statistical framework for inferring cosmological and astrophysical model parameters using SGWB-EM correlations. These techniques were developed and described in three refereed journal papers. Furthermore, in the latest of the papers, the techniques were applied to the most recent gravitational wave data from the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors, and to the Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxy catalog data, resulting in the first measurements of the SGWB-galaxy count angular power spectrum. The measurements were then used to infer constraints on parameters describing the population of binary black hole systems, which is the first study of its kind. More recently, the techniques are also being applied to the Euclid simulated galaxy count surveys, in preparation for the upcoming Euclid survey data.

This project brought together experts on gravitational wave astrophysics (both observers and theorists) with experts in traditional (electromagnetic) astronomy and large scale structure formation. As such, the project has developed ties between the two respective communities, which are expected to further develop with the arrival of Euclid data and with more senstive gravitational wave data from LIGO, Virgo, and Kagra detectors. Graduate and undergraduate students participating in the project had opportunities to closely work with these experts at the intersection of the two fields, and to play leading roles in pioneering new analysis techniques and in publishing respective papers. With such exposure, they are well positioned to make a significant impact on the field, which will also reflect in their future careers.

abstractText:
This project is led by Professor Connie Lu of the University of Minnesota and is funded by the Chemical Catalysis program of the Chemistry Division. The main goal of this project is to convert carbon dioxide, a gas found in volcanoes, hot springs and geysers, as well as in deposits of petroleum and natural gas, into fuels.  Professor Lu is testing new catalysts for this chemical conversion. The catalysts used in this research are formed from pairs of metals.  Notably, some pairs, such as iron and aluminium, are promising candidates to accelerate the desired reactions, while other pairs are less active.  The Lu team focuses on determining the structures of the active pairs. This research develops the foundations for the design of future catalysts and renewable fuels.  Students gain international experience and exposure to US National Laboratories through short research stays at the Max Planck Institute in Germany and the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, as well as site visits to Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.  These enriching opportunities build a stronger, more experienced US workforce.  Professor Lu and her team volunteer in the student-led program, SciMentors, which helps underserved adult learners pass the GED exam through tutoring and hands-on science experiments. This project contributes to scientific literacy and addresses economic competitiveness of the U.S.

Advances in catalyst design increasingly focus on the use of base metals because of their low cost and low environmental footprint. Funded by NSF's Chemical Catalysis Program, Professor Connie Lu of the University of Minnesota is investigating Lewis acidic sigma-acceptor metalloligands to enable new modes of reactivity at a base metal by leveraging the M→LA bonding interaction between the base metal (M) and the Lewis acid (LA). Recently, M−LA complexes have emerged as an important class of bifunctional catalysts, where the LA has predominantly been a main group ion. For this project, Professor Lu and her team are targeting M-LA catalysts centered on base metals (Fe, Co, and Ni) and lanthanide ions to achieve the hydrogenation of CO2 to formate, and ultimately, to methanol. The team also aims to expand the catalytic scope of these bifunctional complexes by targeting C-C bond formation processes that leverage the unique cooperativity of the M-LA active site.

projectOutComesReport:
The outcomes of this project spanned a wide variety of chemistries that connected inorganic and organic synthesis and catalysis. Catalysis is important to society by allowing for efficient use of resources to build chemicals that society needs. Catalysts lower the energy need to perform a reaction which is an essential energy-saving process. This project contributed to this larger goal by developing potentially new catalyst designs that may change how certain chemicals are currently being made. These include ways to make carbon-carbon bonds that are found in agrochemicals, fine chemicals, and pharmaceuticals. The starting materials for these reactions were from naturally occurring carboxylic acids derivatives or cheap and readily available sodium salts. Additionally, catalysts were developed that were bifunctional-meaning a single catalyst had two different roles in a catalytic reaction. This bifunctionality allowed the catalyst to perform two critical roles in the catalytic cycle - both the binding of a substrate as well as activation of a bond. These cataysts contained earth abundant metals such as copper and cobalt, which are needed to replace transition metal catalysts that contain metals that are scarce. 

This grant also supported two students who did internships at a national lab and in industry. These internship opportunities are essential for preparing students for the chemistry workforce. Ample opportunities were also provided to present at national meetings as well as specific meetings supporting underrepresented STEM students.

abstractText:
The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted public health with a large number of mortalities and ravaged the economy by increasing unemployment to a historically high level. The goal of this project is to investigate the potential for novel spatiotemporal big data to assist in identifying COVID-19 related geographic patterns, such as locations where groups of people visit for long, overlapping times, and travel to and from hotspots. Such patterns are of great interest to policy-makers and public health researchers, but are difficult to find in traditional mobility datasets such as infrequent travel surveys and urban highway traffic data. Example spatiotemporal big data include privacy-protected aggregated location traces of mobile devices that have recently been opened for COVID-19 research. If successful, the results will inform disease spread models and policy-interventions to save lives and reopen the economy safely.

This project is expected to result in multiple data science and computer science innovations. First, it will define and quantify hangout-venues, a novel spatiotemporal pattern family modeling the places with many overlapping long visits. Examples include full-service dine-in restaurants which have many long visits, but not limited-service restaurants which mostly have short visits. Second, it will probe new interest measures to not only distinguish between patterns (e.g., full-service restaurants) and non-patterns (e.g., limited-service restaurants) but also support the design of computationally efficient algorithms based on properties such as anti-monotone. Third, it will design novel and scalable algorithms for analyzing the large (tens of terabytes) dataset for hangout-venues. Fourth, it will investigate the impact of selection bias and noise from differential privacy schemes. The results have the potential to transform data science knowledge with novel pattern families (e.g., hangout-venue) and improve the understanding of the impact of selection bias and noise added by differential privacy schemes on pattern mining methods and their results. Furthermore, the project will co-produce knowledge in close collaboration with public health researchers and policymakers. The results have the potential to transform the understanding of the public mobility for modeling disease transmission dynamics by leveraging the emerging spatiotemporal big data.

orgLongName: Directorate for Computer and Information Science and Engineering
program: INFO INTEGRATION & INFORMATICS, EAGER
projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic has greatly impacted public health and the economy since 2020 by disrupting hospitals and supply chains. A key COVID-19 policy intervention in Minnesota in the early days of the pandemic was stay-at-home orders issued by the governor. This project investigated the potential for novel geospatial big data and inform policymakers to reduce disease spread and safely reopen the economy in the context of questions such as: (a) What were the mobility impacts of COVID-19 policy interventions (e.g., stay-at-home)? How did the impact vary over time and place? (b) Which points of interest and business categories had the most long-duration visits? Examples of the newly available geospatial big data include privacy-protected aggregated location traces of mobile devices from the SafeGraph COVID-19 consortium. To interpret the pros and cons of the new dataset, the project also addressed questions such as: (a) How does the dataset protect the individual's privacy? (b) What is the sampling rate? (c) How does the mobile device data compare with other well-known datasets?

This project resulted in many new insights. First, we improved understanding of the geospatial mobility data analysis questions of interest. Our analysis of Minnesota mobility data from the SafeGraph COVID-19 consortium showed that bars and full-service restaurants had many more long-duration visits than limited-service restaurants. It also showed that the number of visits to parks (and hardware stores) went up while the number of visits to airports, schools, workplaces, malls, etc., went down during the stay-at-home period. Another finding was that the distances traveled diminished for Minnesota suburbanites but not for downtown residents, possibly due to differences in commutes before and during the stay-at-home order.  Second, we analyzed the strengths and weaknesses of the Safegraph mobility datasets which summarizes the movement of large samples of smartphones. This type of data is promising in transportation research due to the high frequency of data collection and the high geographic coverage relative to traditional loop detector and travel survey data. However, we found the sampling rate (ratio between sampled devices and population) varies across different census tracts in Minnesota. In addition, the dataset does not report demographic distribution by age, gender, race, etc.

 Due to their timeliness and significance, the project results were presented to the Minnesota State House Transportation Finance and Policy Committee on January 14th, 2021, to inform a hearing on COVID-19's impact on the future of transportation. Also, technical details were peer-reviewed and presented at the 2022 Annual Conference of the Association of Geographic Information Laboratories in Europe (AGILE), the Computing Research Association (CRA) Virtual Conference 2020, the National Science Foundation (NSF) Covid Information Commons managed by the Northeast Big-Data Innovation Hub, and the University of Minnesota Center for Transportation Studies annual conference (2020). Furthermore, the project periodically published summary reports based on the SafeGraph COVID-19 consortium data. These reports summarized the number of long-duration visits to different business categories (e.g., bars, limited-service restaurants, full-service restaurants) and points of interest (e.g., Minneapolis-Saint Paul International airport). The details can be found at http://www.spatial.cs.umn.edu/Project/covid_19.html.

This project trained three Ph.D. students in Computer Science and Engineering and provided mentorships for three High School students. In addition, the project enhanced educational experience by providing research projects, hands-on homework and laboratory exercises, and other active learning activities (e.g., class presentations) for students in both graduate and undergraduate courses at the University of Minnesota.
