abstractText:
One of the major intellectual achievements of the 20th century was the development of the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics. This model succeeded in classifying all of the elementary particles known at the time into a hierarchy of groups having similar quantum properties. The validity of this model to date was confirmed by the discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN. However, the Standard Model as it currently exists leaves open many questions about the universe, including such fundamental questions as to why the Higgs mass has the value it has and why there is no antimatter in the universe. A primary area to search for answers to these and other open questions about the universe, how it came to be and why it is the way it is, is to focus on a study of the properties of neutrinos and to use what we know and can learn about neutrinos as probes of science beyond the Standard Model. Neutrinos are those elementary particles that interact with practically nothing else in the universe. They have no electric charge and were once thought to be massless. Like other elementary particles, they were believed to have an antimatter counterpart, the antineutrino. Moreover, the Standard Model predicted that there were actually three different kinds of neutrinos that were distinguishable through the different interactions that they did undergo whenever there was an interaction. But recent measurements have totally changed our picture of neutrinos. We now know that neutrinos do have a mass and because they do, they can actually change from one type to another. The Intellectual Merit of this work is in the detailed measurements of these changes, along with other current neutrino experiments.  These form one of the most promising ways to probe for new physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) and are the subject of this investigation. This research will involve the work of undergraduate students at the University of Minnesota, Duluth, an RUI. 

Faculty and students working on the NOvA and MINERvA experiments will further the neutrino oscillation measurements and are working toward first astrophysics results. The effort includes enhancing the ability for NOvA electronics to self-detect the neutrino burst from a potential galactic supernova and share that alert with the world-wide supernova detection network. Neutrino interaction measurements continue with existing and incoming data from the MINERvA experiment. Finally, the group is pursuing work toward the next generation experiment, DUNE, including roles in the data acquisition system, design of the near detectors, and the role of neutrino interaction uncertainties in the design sensitivity of the experiment. This grant also supports broader impacts via participation and leadership of the  NOvA outreach program, which includes regular summer tours of the Soudan Underground Laboratory and the NOvA detector at the Ash River, MN site.

projectOutComesReport:
During this grant, the PIs and numerous students made significant contributions to the study of neutrino interactions, neutrino oscillations, and particle astrophysics.  Analysis of MINERvA data and effort with interaction models clarifies the expected energy dependence of neutrino reactions with nuclei.   The energy dependence of these processes are central to neutrino oscillation experiments such as NOvA and T2K as well as DUNE and SBN.  In 2023, MINERvA published a major result in Nature on the neutrino axial form factor where prior work from one PI and students played a central role.  The other PI and students published papers using NOvA data to study cosmic rays and search for magnetic monopoles and astrophysical neutrinos.   The PI’s were also leaders on their experiments.   Gran served as co-convenor of the DUNE interaction uncertainties working group, which is upgrading the interaction model and systematics to support the Near Detector technical design decisions.  Habig was co-convenor of NOvA's Exotics working group, director of the Ash River NOvA Far Detector Facility, and co-convenor of the DUNE DAQ Facilities and integration working group.   In addition to the broader impacts from training the next generation of scientists and engineers through research experiences, we hosted two International Particle Physics Master Classes as part of this grant.

title: RUI: Experimental Neutrino Research at Minnesota Duluth

abstractText:
Covid-19 has spread rapidly since it was detected in Hubei province in China. To estimate potential impact of Covid-19, researchers have employed models to predict numbers of people infected, and the potential morbidity caused by the virus.  Importantly, results from models guide policies for controlling the spread of the COVID-19 virus, where it is also recognized that conclusions reached vary considerably based on the model being employed. Here, for effective mitigation and prediction of the spread of the virus it is important to construct the transmission network of COVID-19 which informs the routes the virus takes in introducing or re-introducing infections to different regions and populations. An accurate estimate of the transmission network will help in developing models with higher fidelity and accuracy and can help in effective mitigation strategies.  The project will develop a data-driven approach for reconstruction of transmission network of COVID-19, to complement and aid model-based approaches. Here, relative interdependence and independence of infection in a region from other infections in other regions estimated solely from data history will be employed. Such a data-driven approach has the potential to evolve significant complementary insights and guide strategies for COVID-19 mitigation.

There are numerous parametric models being employed to analyze/predict evolution of the Covid-19 based viral infection. In this project, the focus is to unravel the evolution of the transmission network of infections as inferred from data. A primary approach is based on filtering and multivariate optimal estimation. The first step of the methodology is to identify the pathway by which an agent can affect another agent where all intermediate agents that facilitate transmission of infection from one agent to another are identified. In the second step the focus is on estimating the dynamics of the transmission whereby aspects such as the delay in expression of infection from the time the agent encounters an infected agent are unraveled. Tools from graphical models and their relationship to filtering over networks will be brought to bear on the problem. The data-driven algorithms are agnostic to models bringing complimentary set of insights into the Covid-19 transmission from the model-based approaches currently being employed. The filtering/optimization-based methods will be used on data generated by standard epidemiological models such as the Susceptible-Infected-Removed models.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Covid-19 epidemic has further motivated research on how to reach meaningful inferences from time-series data. Here quantities such as the number of infections and recovery with respect to time and location are recorded and analyzed and methods are targeted to gain useful insights toward factors that govern the flow of influences. A key feature of many time-series data is that data being collected from multiple sources are often dynamically related, for example, the influence of one source of data on another is often accompanied by delays.  This project focused on methods and algorithms to unravel the flow of influence from data that is dynamically related. The project resulted in methods for unravelling the topology of influences for data that has statistics that may be changing with time. Another key focus of the project was on problems where there are latent variables which are not monitored or measured; the underlying challenge is to understand how different agents interact when some of the agents remain hidden. Under this project, conditions are identified which when met can allow the number of underlying latent variables to be determined and the relationships between the observed sources and latent sources of data can be unveiled. Another key aspect researched under the project is to determine bounds on the size of the data that is needed to reach meaningful assertions on the topology of influences. The project has led to software, has trained graduate students and has led to publications in leading journals. The project has led to content to new courses.

abstractText:
The geological history of tropical glaciers can provide scientists an important perspective from the past on how Earth’s climate system responds to human activity. This project will look to the geological record of tropical glaciers in the Andes Mountains for a perspective on past changes in the glacial ice extent and how these changes may relate to records of changes in the atmospheric conditions during periods of abrupt climate change. These records of glacial activity will help place the current state of rapidly retreating ice margins in the tropics in a longer-term context that extends well beyond the instrumental record. Finally, by integrating multiple archives of past climates and modeling the causes of tropical high elevation climate changes, this work will improve our understanding of abrupt global climate changes because these regions had much larger glaciers in the past. By determining ages on the rocks that were transported by the ancient glaciers and combining analyses of lake sediments deposited continuously below the glaciers, this research will provide a detailed record of how much the glaciers changed and when. The research team will incorporate climate model simulations to test the causes of tropical climate changes and how they relate to high latitude warming and cooling events. This project will train 3 graduate students, and at least 4 undergraduate students. The project team will improve K-12 science education and engagement by exposing teachers and students (both local and abroad) to research through the GLOBE program (Global Learning and Observation to Benefit the Environment). The team also will partner with INAIGEM in Peru to broaden project impact, and help with the mission of educational capacity building.
 
This project will evaluate tropical glacial variability during the local Last Glacial Maximum (LLGM) to better understand how low latitude temperature variability and the hydrologic cycle were modulated by ocean and atmospheric processes. This research has the following objectives: 1) determine robust ages of moraines using terrestrial cosmogenic radionuclide (TCN) dating methods to provide information about both the timing and extent of multiple LLGM ice limits; 2) rigorously evaluate centennial-scale records of glacial flour flux using high-resolution geochemical archives from the recently acquired Lake Junín drill-core record; 3) test the scale and climatic forcing of LLGM climate variability using climate model simulations; 4) test the scale of LLGM glacier variability responses to climatic forcing using energy and mass-balance models. This research will produce multi-proxy, centennial-scale records of mountain glaciation in Peru spanning the LLGM, at a scale and resolution that has not yet been achieved. This resolution will be sufficient to make comparisons with ice cores from Greenland, Antarctica, and the tropical Andes, as well as decadal-scale speleothem-based stable isotope records of hydroclimate changes from the same (Lake Junín) catchment. This will allow for a collective evaluation of mountain glacier archives and other regional records of past atmospheric variability that will improve our understanding of the role of the tropics in abrupt global change events on millennial timescales. These records will provide insight on the sensitivity of tropical glaciers to a range of climate conditions, both atmospheric and oceanic, and particularly how the tropical climate system responds to meltwater forcing. Ultimately, these records will inform how the tropical hydrologic cycle drives glacial-interglacial cycles in both the low and high latitudes.

projectOutComesReport:
Tropical mountain glaciers are among the most sensitive indicators of climate change, yet their past responses to major climate shifts remain poorly understood. This project used advanced climate and glacier modeling to investigate how changes in global climate influenced glaciers in the tropical Andes during the Last Local Glacial Maximum (approximately 35,000–19,000 years ago), with a focus on the Junín region of central Peru.

A major outcome of the project was the application of state-of-the-art Earth system models to simulate past climate conditions, including changes in greenhouse gases, solar radiation, and ocean circulation. These simulations were used to test how disruptions in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) affected tropical temperatures and rainfall. Results show that changes in ocean circulation can strongly influence tropical climate, helping explain why glacier advances in the Andes were sometimes out of phase with climate changes in the Northern Hemisphere.

The project also advanced the use of isotope-enabled climate models to interpret oxygen isotope records from tropical ice cores. Model–data comparisons revealed strong agreement during the deglaciation but unexpected differences during the Holocene, highlighting limitations in how current models represent key climate feedbacks such as snow and ice albedo. These findings motivated new high-resolution simulations designed to improve how precipitation isotopes are represented over mountainous terrain.

To link climate changes to glacier behavior, the project employed physically based glacier energy and mass-balance models. These models demonstrated that local topography can strongly modulate glacier response, causing neighboring glaciers to react differently to the same climate forcing. This insight improves interpretations of glacial landforms and strengthens reconstructions of past climate conditions.

Beyond scientific advances, the project provided significant training opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, who gained experience in climate modeling, glacier simulation, and scientific communication. Overall, this project improved understanding of how global climate processes influence tropical mountain environments and provides important context for ongoing glacier retreat and water-resource challenges in the Andes.

abstractText:
Understanding the evolution of photosynthesis, the process of using light energy to convert carbon dioxide (CO2) into biomass, remains an outstanding question. A number of factors confound our ability to trace the evolution of photosynthesis: associated observed chemical limitations are not clearly defined in genetic information and horizontal gene transfer (the transfer of genetic information between microorganisms) hinders phylogenetic approaches. In the absence of characterized deeply-branching microorganisms, a robust phylogenomic framework, and undisputed biosignatures in the rock record, facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis in extant cyanobacteria represents an opportunity to better understand and constrain the evolution of photosynthesis. In this project, the investigator will characterize photosynthesis in an emerging model cyanobacterium, Leptolyngbya sp. strain hensonii, isolated from an anoxic, sulfide-rich sinkhole. This research will evaluate the genetic response of Leptolyngbya sp. strain hensonii to the presence of sulfide (which has been linked to inhibition of oxygenic photosynthesis) and the potential for a cyanobacterium to express a single photosystem based on environmental conditions. Collectively, the data will provide insight into the physiology and potential success of cyanobacteria prior to the evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis. The study will examine the role of life in the transformation and evolution of Earth's geochemical cycles and the evolution of photosynthesis, which is an outstanding question in geobiology. The project will train a graduate student and an undergraduate student. In addition, the research team will develop a demonstration for Market Science to broadly disseminate findings at Farmers' Markets in and around the Twin Cities area of Minnesota.

The ability to harvest light and fuel cellular processes through phototrophy is arguably one the most important biological innovations in Earth history. Yet, understanding the evolution of photosynthesis remains an outstanding question in geobiology. Oxygenic photosynthesis is often cited as the most important microbial innovation having tipped the scale from a reducing early Earth to an oxygenated world that eventually lead to complex life. However, oxygenic phototrophs use two reaction centers: Photosystem II and Photosystem I for light-driven oxidation of water to fuel primary productivity. In extant sunlit environments where low oxygen concentrations and sulfide persist, some cyanobacteria can use sulfide as the electron donor to photosystem I, performing anoxygenic photosynthesis. In the absence of characterized deeply-branching isolates, a robust phylogenomic framework, and irrefutable biosignatures in the rock record, facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis in extant cyanobacteria represents a tractable system for examining the evolution of photosynthesis including the potential for an early evolving one-photosystem cyanobacterium. The proposed research plan will integrate a set of physiological studies coupled with systems biology approaches—transcriptomics and proteomics—to characterize an emerging model cyanobacterium isolated from a sulfidic, anoxic environment. The following objectives will guide this work: 1) define the molecular machinery necessary for anoxygenic photosynthesis; 2) characterize the effects of sulfide on photosystem II during anoxygenic photosynthesis; 3) determine oxidation kinetics of sulfide during anoxygenic photosynthesis; 4) examine the enhancement of carbon fixation in the presence of sulfide. The proposed research will examine the role of life in the transformation and evolution of Earth's geochemical cycles and the evolution of photosynthesis.

projectOutComesReport:
Understanding the evolution of photosynthesis, the process of using light energy to convert CO2 into biomass, remains an outstanding question. A number of factors confound our ability to trace the evolution of photosynthesis: associated observed chemical limitations are not clearly defined in genetic information and horizontal gene transfer (the transfer of genetic information between microorganisms) hinders phylogenetic approaches. In the absence of characterized deeply-branching microorganisms, a robust phylogenomic framework, and undisputed biosignatures in the rock record, facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis in extant cyanobacteria represents an opportunity to better understand and constrain the evolution of photosynthesis. 

In this project, we characterized facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis in an emerging model cyanobacterium, Leptolyngbya sp. strain hensonii, isolated from an anoxic, sulfide-rich sinkhole. We evaluated how Leptolyngbya sp. strain hensonii responds to the presence of sulfide (which inhibits oxygenic photosynthesis) and the potential for a cyanobacterium to express a single photosystem based on environmental conditions. We characterized anoxygenic photosynthesis in our new isolate, O. malbecolor, and compared these data to those of Leptolyngbya strain hensonii (the original isolate). Both isolates perform facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis in the presence of sulfide, and this activity is highest around 40 μM in sulfide in both isolates (similar to the sulfide concentration in Little Salt Spring). Based on photosynthetic over-irradiance curves, O. malbecolor prefers lower light compared to Leptolyngbya strain hensonii, which might suggest O. malbecolor occupies niche space deeper in the phototrophic mat in Little Salt Spring (Florida, US) compared to Leptolyngbya strain hensonii. Both isolates display elevated gross anoxygenic photosynthesis activity compared to oxygenic photosynthesis. Based on low-temperature emission spectra, both Leptolyngbya strain hensonii and O. malbecolor contain significantly more photosystem I in the presence of sulfide compared to photosystem II, consistent with facultative anoxygenic photosynthesis being a photosystem I-dependent process.

We performed a comparative genome analysis of our new isolate, O. malbecolor to Leptolyngbya strain hensonii (the original isolate). Despite being different species, the two isolates share the majority of functions and appear to be similar physiologically. Both genomes encode all the genes necessary for oxygenic photosynthesis as well as an enzyme for oxidizing sulfide. The genomes also encode the enzymes and gene products necessary to thrive under low oxygen conditions, including oxidases and oxygen-sensitive bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis enzymes.

Collectively, these data provide insight into the physiology and potential success of cyanobacteria before the evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis. These results improve current understanding of the role of life in the transformation and evolution of Earth’s geochemical cycles and the evolution of photosynthesis, which are outstanding questions in geobiology. 

The proposal trained two postdoctoral researchers and three undergraduate students. Postdoctoral researchers received training and mentoring in manuscript and grant proposal preparation. All researchers received training and mentoring in best practices in geobiological research, including experimental design. With the postdoctoral researchers, we developed a robust pipeline for co-assembling long- and short-read genomic sequencing data. Data from this project were incorporated into field and lecture courses, and data were presented through several invited seminars. We also developed activities for a museum summer camp. Published data is available through open-access journal repositories and through the Data Repository for the University of Minnesota (DRUM). All additional data will be shared through the NCBI (long- and short-read sequencing data), through DRUM, and in supplemental material in open-access journals.

abstractText:
From raindrops battering on a windshield to coffee splashing on a table, drop impact is ubiquitous in our daily life and relevant to many important natural and industrial processes. Although the phenomenon has been studied for many decades, the understanding of drop impact is still far from complete due to the complexity associated with typical fast impact processes. Significant progress has been made on drop impact in recent years using high-speed photographic techniques. Relying on direct imaging, most experiments focused on the kinematics of drop impact, i.e., the shape of impacting drops. Few studies have probed the dynamic properties of drop impact such as its impact force, pressure and shear stress. These dynamic quantities lead to the most important outcome of an impact event and affect a wide range of phenomena, including soil erosion, impact-induced wear/damage and the survival of living organisms exposed to the elements. The goal of this research is to conduct a systematic study on mapping the dynamic aspects of drop impact under different conditions. The research will develop a new experimental technique, 3D high-speed stress microscopy, to measure the impact force, pressure, and shear stress of drop impact with high spatial and temporal resolutions. The project will provide a fundamental understanding of the dynamics of drop impact in unexplored regimes and a practical guideline to control impact forces and mitigate impact-induced damage on solid substrates. The project will also provide a unique opportunity to introduce frontier research in undergraduate curriculum and forge collaborations with coating companies. 

By combining traction force microscopy with high-speed photography, the research will construct a 3D high-speed stress microscope to measure the temporal variation of pressure and shear stress distributions beneath an impacting drop during a fast impact process. With the new technique, the project will verify previous theoretical predictions, including the singular dynamics of off-center pressures, the scaling relation of drag forces, and the propagation of boundary layers in spreading drops. As such, the study will reveal the dynamics of drop impact in spatiotemporal regimes, inaccessible to conventional kinematic measurements. Moreover, the research will examine the influence of different surface properties such as stiffness, wettability, and micro-textures on the stress distributions. The study aims to seek optimal surface designs, which can substantially reduce impact-induced wear and damage.

projectOutComesReport:
The impact of a liquid drop on a solid surface is a common yet complex phenomenon, playing a vital role in numerous natural and industrial processes—from soil erosion and aerosol dispersion to inkjet printing and spray coating. Understanding the dynamics of drop impact is both fundamentally intriguing and practically significant. On a fundamental level, drop impact serves as a key model for examining the intricate interplay of forces that govern fluid flow across various length and time scales. Insights from such studies can significantly enhance our understanding of fluid dynamics. Practically, controlling drop impact outcomes is essential for optimizing industrial coating and printing techniques. Consequently, drop impact has been one of the most extensively studied topics in fluid dynamics, with research dating back over a century to Worthington's pioneering work.

Among the various aspects of drop impact, its dynamical features—specifically, the impact force and stress of the drops—have been less explored due to the lack of suitable experimental techniques. In this project, we developed new methods to measure the temporal evolution of impact forces, as well as the pressure and shear stress distributions beneath impacting drops. We applied these techniques to study the impact of both Newtonian and non-Newtonian drops and further extended our research to investigate the scaling relation of the maximum spreading of impacting drops.

This project yielded three significant results. First, we developed a novel method called high-speed stress microscopy to capture the rapid evolution of pressure and shear stress distributions beneath millimeter-sized drops at varying impact velocities. Our findings revealed that the maximum pressure and shear stress propagate along with the contact line at a speed exceeding the speed of sound in the impacted surface during the early stages of impact. This leads to the formation of a shock wave, causing considerable surface wear. Second, we devised a numerical method to simulate the impact of non-Newtonian shear-thinning and shear-thickening drops. By integrating these simulations with experimental data on different non-Newtonian fluids, we investigated how the maximum impact forces depend on the rheological properties of these fluids. Notably, we established a correlation between the relaxation time of the fluids and the maximum impact force. Finally, we explored the maximum spreading behavior of both Newtonian and non-Newtonian drops. Our results challenge the established understanding of how the maximum spreading depends on various impact parameters, revealing a new regime with previously overlooked scaling laws. Overall, our findings significantly advance the understanding of drop impact dynamics and introduce a powerful tool for measuring previously unexplored aspects of this phenomenon. Additionally, our work offers valuable insights for controlling drop impact outcomes, such as the extent of spreading and impact-induced damage and wear.

Our work has resulted in two publications in highly-ranked journals: one in Nature Communications and the other in the Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics. Additionally, we are preparing two more manuscripts to report findings from the latter stages of the project. A graduate student supported by this project has successfully completed their Ph.D., with their thesis published. The grant also supported five presentations at national and international conferences, and the PI delivered several seminars on the topic at various institutions. These activities have been instrumental in disseminating our results within both academic and industrial communities. Particularly, our work has garnered significant interest from the coating industry, fostering opportunities for future collaborations. Finally, the grant has also supported the PI's outreach efforts. Our results have been featured by several news outlets, including an interview on WTIP 90.7 North Shore Community Radio, helping to raise public awareness of science and engineering. The PI also mentored the University of Minnesota's Energy Club and organized science demonstrations for pre-K children at the University of Minnesota Child Development Center, further promoting interest in research among the general public.

abstractText:
Random thermal fluctuations can form knots in polymers such as DNA much like shaking headphones can cause knots in the cord.  As a result, knots are common in long polymer chains. Knots also can be created by fluid flow. The objective of this project is to perform experiments that uncover how a knot is formed in a flow and how it is removed after formation. Broadly speaking, knotted polymers are important both to fundamental problems in biology and to applied topics in biotechnology. The immediate technological impacts of this problem lie in two emerging long-read genomics technologies: genome mapping and nanopore sequencing. Knotting in DNA also has a broader importance in biology, in particular for regulation of the genome.

This project experimentally addresses two key scientific questions related to knotting of long polymers, using DNA as a model system. The first part focuses on how stalling DNA at a nanofluidic interface produces knots, focusing on developing mechanistic insights via fluorescence microscopy. The second part focuses on the transport properties of DNA knots. These experiments leverage nanochannels as a “hydrodynamic microscope” to isolate the hydrodynamic interactions within the knot from hydrodynamic interactions between the knot and the rest of the chain. Through this work, graduate students on the project will receive training in clean-room fabrication methods, fluorescence microscopy, image processing, and the theories of hydrodynamics and polymer physics. This project also involves a K-12 outreach project to develop science fair projects related to the research for high school students.

projectOutComesReport:
Knots are a familiar object in our daily lives, from the simple knots you use to tie your shoes to the more complex knots used for sailing. Polymers, which are large molecules that consist of many repeat chemical units, can also form knots at the macromolecular scale. The knots can form simply due to the thermal energy of the fluid containing the polymer, or they can be created by active processes such as fluid flow. DNA, the molecule that encodes the genetic makeup of every living organism, is an especially important polymer that can form knots. Regulation of these knots is so important that there exists a set of enzymes called topoisomerases that control the topology of DNA in cells. Knotting also plays a confounding role in next-generation genomics technologies that require stretching out DNA to observe sequence-dependent features of the molecule.

This project used experiments and computer simulations to understand how knots move along DNA molecules. The experiments leveraged a microfluidic technology known as the "knot factory", which was fabricated using the same technologies used to create computer chips, to create large complex knots on DNA that can be visualized using fluorescence microscopy. The first part of the project probed the mechanism that a single knot moves on DNA, testing two hypotheses: (i) a self-reptation mechanism, where the DNA moves in a snake-like fashion along the knot, and (ii) knot breathing, where the knot opens and closes as it moves along the DNA. Experimental results suggested that the self-reptation mechanism was dominant based on the way that the random fluctuations fo the knot position evolved in time, but subsequent simulations showed that both mechanisms are active and simply using the evolution of the knot position in time is insufficient. The second part of the project measured the friction of the knot on DNA when constrained in a channel. The knot reduces the total length of the DNA molecule, which would reduce the overall friction. However, the knot also puts more DNA close to the channel walls, which would increase the overall friction. The experiments clearly showed that the wall friction contribution dominated. The third part of the project measured the interactions between two knots on a DNA molecule. The experiments showed that there is an attraction between the two knots, but they do not remain in close proximity or intertwine. The attraction for the confined knots is akin to what is observed for two knots on DNA that is stretched in flow, but the flow-based system (where the molecule is in tension) lead to knots that stay in close proximity for long times. This apparent contradiction was resolved by simulations of two knots on DNA molecules. For the simplest knot, the trefoil (which looks like a pretzel), two knots in DNA can intertwine down to very small channel sizes. However, the next most complicated knot topology only intertwines at channel sizes that are similar to the experiments. Since the knot factory produces large, complicated knots, the simulations confirmed the experimental result. Moreover, through careful control of the knot topology in the simulations and comparisons of intertwining in stretched double-knotted DNA, the suppression of intertwining was confirmed to be due to the channel walls suppressing the transverse fluctuations of the DNA.

This project involved a postdoctoral researcher, a graduate student, an undergraduate student, and two high school students. All these participants received training in advanced scientific skills, including high performance computation, microfabrication, fluorescence microscopy, and manipulation of large DNA molecules. This project also contributed to increasing the gender diversity of the scientific workforce; of the five participants, four of them identify as female. Training of this type at all educational stages is important for the maintenance of the technology workforce in the US.

abstractText:
PART 1: NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Ready access to clean water is a pressing global challenge that represents one of the most important sustainability issues we face as a society. Desalination of sea water and wastewater remediation/reuse are two prevalent solutions that will benefit from new advances in basic materials research. These approaches to generating clean water for consumption rely on the use of membranes endowed with material properties designed to optimize separations performance. This research project focuses on new state-of-the-art polymeric materials designed to address key limitations that must be overcome to further advance understanding and efficacy of materials used in membrane-based separations. The objectives are to design and advance the use of block polymer materials for membranes using a combination of contemporary polymer synthesis, thorough materials characterization, and integration of new macromolecules into practical separation membranes. The research promises to benefit society through the eventual development of new technologies that render water purification and remediation more economical and more widely accessible. Membranes will play important roles in a sustainable water future and the fundamental underpinnings achieved in this work will help solidify the foundations from which new technologies will be built. The work will also build diverse STEM talent though partnerships that include the NorthStar STEM Alliance, American Chemical Society’s Project SEED, and the University of Minnesota's Science for All group.


PART 2: TECHNICAL SUMMARY

The research work centers around the design, development, and deployment of block polymer centric strategies that rely on the self-assembly of novel compounds to take advantage of their nanostructured morphologies. Co-continuous nanostructures are essential to advance the design of materials for next-generation water purification membranes, and this research will advance knowledge useful for the creation of co-continuous nanostructured polymer materials that are useful for aqueous-based separations. The essential feature of the program emphasizes the preparation of materials with co-continuous nanostructures by capitalizing on the disordered state of block polymer derived materials. The work will advance knowledge in two main categories. The first is based on a thermodynamic approach that entails trapping a disordered co-continuous morphology in the thermodynamically stable disordered state using pre-formed block polymers. The second is based on a kinetic approach that entails trapping the disordered state during the in-situ synthesis of block polymers in a system that is conducive to chemical fixation through crosslinking. The fundamental and basic research efforts will advance knowledge in these two arenas, will contribute to the basic understanding of block polymer thermodynamics, and will ultimately allow for new technologies to be built that contribute to sustainable access to clean water.

projectOutComesReport:
The design, development, and deployment of new polymeric materials useful for various types of separations is a critical research endeavor. This National Science Foundation grant supported our work focused on using a particular class of specialty polymers called block polymers. These macromolecules contain two or more distinct components that endow them with remarkable chemical and physical properties and that result in materials with a tunable array of attractive characteristics. The bulk of our work under this award focused on the careful design of block polymers such that they adopted a particular structure on the nanoscale. Specifically, we designed systems that formed interwoven domains of polymeric species that permeated the entire material. These so-called bicontinuous structures are incredibly useful in, for example, membranes that are both mechanically robust and can also facilitate transport of liquids such as water. In several examples, we showed that if one of the domains can be selectively removed from the bicontinuous structures, nanoscopic pores that percolate the entire material can be generated. These materials can be used in numerous applications that include the selective removal of impurities (e.g., viruses and other pathogens) from water with membrane technologies (e.g., in wastewater remediation). These approaches to generating clean water for consumption rely on the use of membranes endowed with material properties designed to optimize separations performance.

In addition to our work on porous materials, we also made several advances in nanostructure materials containing ionically charged domains. In this work, we discovered a new method for the generation of materials that simultaneously contained oppositely charged anionic and cationic domains in a single functionalization step. The work is critically important for the formation of a unique class of materials useful in water desalination called charge mosaic membranes that can selectively remove dissolved salts from water. We did this by designing and preparing functional block polymer that could readily self-assembly into interesting and useful nanostructures. 

During this award we also recognized the need to develop even more robust polymeric materials using the modern tools of chemistry. To this end, we showed that we could use a single catalyst not only for the polymerization chemistry, but also for the chemical modification of the product polymers that rendered them much more chemically resistant while also allow for the integration of chemical handles for further functionalization. This major advance has led to new research endeavors and new lines of investigation that will be important for the development of unique materials with many practical outlets. 

We have made numerous fundamental materials research contributions under this grant that have been published in the top peer-reviewed journals.

The direct basic research science outcomes from this award were complemented by broader impacts of the award that went beyond the scientific findings. For example, some of our research efforts led to materials useful for the compatibilization of mixed plastic waste in recycling enabling more strategic and sustainable methods for handling plastic waste at the end of life. We were also successful in building Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) talent through researcher training under this award. Several researchers supported were also from underrepresented groups in the sciences thus helping diversity the STEM workforce. We also made several contributions to scientific outreach and polymer science education. 

In sum, we have advanced the use of block polymer materials for use in membranes using a combination of contemporary polymer synthesis, careful and thorough materials characterization and developed new materials for practical separation membranes. This award enabled not only important scientific discoveries but also had broader implications for society, the STEM workforce, and polymer science training and education.

abstractText:
Part 1: NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Derived from linking two or more polymers with different chemical structures, block polymers are an important class of specialty materials that self-organize into repeating patterns at the nanometer (1/100,000,000 of an inch) length scale. Applications of these structurally periodic materials include advanced water purification membranes, templates for petrochemical refining catalysts, and pattern transfer materials for next-generation integrated circuits. Within an interdisciplinary research environment situated at the crossroads of chemistry, chemical engineering, and materials science, this research project will broadly train young scientists and engineers in hypothesis-driven, rational design of block polymer materials with specific physical attributes. Project participants will use precision synthesis techniques to make new block polymers, in order to probe their nanoscale structures and consequent properties. A key goal of this project is to develop approaches to direct polymer self-organization into periodic line and dot patterns with spacings less than 20 nm, with potential applications for integrated circuit manufacture. Project participants will also engage in scientific demonstration activities for K-8 audiences to cultivate an appreciation for the unusual yet useful properties of polymers, with the aim of broadening participation of traditionally under-represented groups in STEM fields. Additional outreach activities focus on enhancing science literacy around contemporary issues related to plastic waste, recycling, and sustainable plastics use.


Part 2: TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Block polymer self-assembly presents opportunities for molecular design of technologically-relevant materials with spatially periodic nanoscale domains, which stem from the frustrated free energy balance established by covalently linking immiscible polymer segments into a single macromolecule. In linear A/B multiblock polymers, ordered phase selection, stability, and microdomain periodicity depend on polymer composition, degree of polymerization (N), and the energy penalty associated with unfavorable A/B segment contacts. The choice of monomer chemistry sets the A/B contact energy, thereby dictating a minimum N for melt-phase self-assembly and a lower bound on the periodicities of their nanoscale morphologies. Applications of such periodic patterns in nanomanufcaturing of next-generation integrated circuit and bit-patterned data storage media have stimulated development of linear block polymers, which form sub-10 nm features. The ability of brush polymers, in which polymer side chains are densely grafted from a polymer backbone, to assemble at sub-20 nm length scales is less well-explored. This project focuses on detailed studies of molecular structure/self-assembly relationships in core-shell block brush (csBB) polymers, which arise from linking ABA triblock polymers through their chain midpoints. New csBB polymers will be synthesized and characterized by X-ray scattering, rheology, and electron microscopy, in order to quantify how their architecture-induced ordering power depends on the backbone length and structure, and side-chain segmental dispersity. Additionally, fundamental surface wetting and thin film self-assembly characteristics of csBBs will be compared to those of their linear triblock analogues, potentially informing future nanotemplating applications. 
.

projectOutComesReport:
Polymers are key components in numerous useful technologies, including membranes for water purification and selective chemical separations, templates for porous catalysts in petrochemical refining, and semiconductor patterning for microelectronic chip manufacture. Such applications of polymers take advantage of the ability to tailor their specific physical and chemical properties, by changing the molecular-level building blocks from which they are constructed. This award focused on transformative strategies for tailoring the structures that polymers form at the nanometer length scale (1/80,000th of the thickness of a human hair), which underlie their useful properties. The long-term impact of this research is that it provides a potentially universal molecular design roadmap for producing polymers that form precise nanoscale structures, which may enable low-cost advances in the production of new membranes for difficult yet important chemical separations, advanced optical materials for quantum computing, and next-generation nanotemplates to produce faster microchips.

Intellectual merit: 

This research project explored new molecular architectures for controlling the physical properties of block copolymers, which derive from covalently linking polymers with different chemical compositions. The properties of these materials differ from those of their parent segments, because segment immiscibility drives their separation to form various nanoscale structures. While many past studies have focused on the stabilities and types of nanostructures formed by linear block copolymers, fewer studies have investigated the physical properties of nonlinear block copolymers. We developed a scalable method for producing polymers with a “core-shell bottlebrush” architecture, in which a polymer backbone is densely decorated with linear AB diblock copolymers. We examined how the linear density of AB diblock pendants and their chemical compositions influence nanoscale pattern formation and thermal stability. Crucially, this research quantified how “core-shell bottlebrush” molecular architectures drive nanostructure formation at smaller length scales than linear diblock copolymers of the same chemistry. Key findings were disseminated in peer-reviewed scientific publications, and oral and poster presentations to scientific, industrial, and general audiences.

Broader impact:

Situated at the nexus of materials science, chemistry, and chemical engineering, this award significantly broadened participation in STEM disciplines by enabling versatile training of five (5) graduate and three (3) undergraduate students in synthesis, characterization, and processing of use-inspired polymeric materials. Undergraduate materials science education was augmented by incorporating portions of this research into courses in thermodynamics and polymer science. Project personnel also engaged local communities through various science outreach events, including developing “elevator pitches” for general audiences to highlight key concepts and applications of this research, “hands on” demonstrations of the properties of polymers for 8th-12th grade audiences, and participation in science demonstrations showcasing principles in thermodynamics.

abstractText:
The bottom-up construction of synthetic cells that emulate specific biological functions has the potential to address certain societal problems related to human health and the environment. A serious limitation in the current state-of-the-art production of synthetic cells is the lack of basic knowledge of how particular membrane-associated functions can be engineered into the cells. Indeed, integrating membrane functions into synthetic cells requires a quantitative understanding of basic aspects of membrane-protein interactions and dynamics. The goal of this collaborative project is to advance our fundamental understanding of membrane protein functions in genetically programmed synthetic cells using a cutting-edge sensor technology.  This project, which is a collaboration between the University of Minnesota-Twin Cities (US) and the University of Exeter (UK), also aims to provide early career scientists with opportunities to do interdisciplinary research and to introduce cutting-edge biotechnology into the classroom of undergraduate students.   

This interdisciplinary project will provide novel quantitative information on various dynamic features of membrane proteins and their self-assembly by applying highly-sensitive whispering gallery mode single-molecule sensors to a set of three biological membrane functions recapitulated in a synthetic cell system: membrane channels, cytoskeleton and two-component signal transduction systems. The single molecule experiments will be paralleled by a quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation approach to provide complementary information on large scales and collective effects of membrane proteins at the lipid bilayer. The research effort is divided into three objectives, to be carried out during the three-year project. First, the synthetic cell, consisting of a liposome loaded with a cell-free expression reaction to express the membrane proteins, will be set up on the single molecule sensor to monitor the insertion of native membrane protein channels and to characterize their activity. Second, we will use the whispering gallery mode sensors and the microbalance to monitor previously inaccessible adsorption kinetics of cytoskeletal proteins that mediate cell shape and division at the membrane of synthetic cell, as a function of lipid membrane properties. Third, the single molecule experiments will be performed by several independent sensing channels to characterize in real time biomolecular structural changes during signaling of a two-component system. Nanoseconds to hour’s detection timescales of sensor channels will provide information to analyze the hierarchy of protein motions in two component systems signaling, with respect to physical and chemical stimuli. The microbalance will provide information on the relationship between the membrane biophysical and biochemical properties of the membrane and the interaction between the proteins of the two-component system. This project will support the interdisciplinary training of undergraduates and post-doctoral researchers and aspects of the project will be integrated into curriculum of an undergraduate student course.

This collaborative US/UK project is supported by the US National Science Foundation and the UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

projectOutComesReport:
Building synthetic cells (SCs) that mimic specific biological functions holds strong promises as potential solutions to societal problems related to human health and the environment. One of the major approaches to assemble SCs from natural molecular components consists of encapsulating a cell-free transcription-translation system (TXTL) into liposomes. TXTL is a reconstituted cytoplasm, the liquid solution inside cells from which it’s genomic DNA has been removed. It is a physiological solution that contains all the molecular components necessary to achieve the expression of genes encoded into DNA prepared in the laboratory. Liposomes are spherical cell-sized compartments (1-20 µm in diameter) made of a closed lipid membrane, similar to real living cells. Such an experimental setting is used by experimentalists to build SCs that emulate specific biological functions, to understand the biological and biophysical mechanisms at play in living cells, as well as to develop potential applications. Developing elaborated biological functions at the membrane is one of the current bottlenecks in SCs research. Integral and interacting membrane proteins (IIMPs) constitute a vast family of biomolecules that perform essential functions in all forms of life, such as sensing and selective uptake and export of metabolites. Yet, characterizing their interactions with the lipid membrane of SCs remains limited due to challenges, such as the labeling of IIMPs without disrupting their function.

In this project, we used a quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCMD) to establish a non-disruptive approach to characterizing the interactions of IIMPs, synthesized using TXTL, with lipid membranes adsorbed onto the QCMD sensor surface. A QCMD is a highly sensitive scale that measures the mass added to a surface in real time. The combined TXTL-QCMD approach enables the non-disruptive characterization of IIMP interactions with a lipid membrane.

We showed that membranes with arbitrary lipid compositions can be made on the QCMD surface, and we generated a broad variety of membranes with lipids compositions of biological relevance. We characterized the interactions TXTL with the lipid membranes and demonstrated that TXTL components show remarkedly low non-specific adsorption onto lipid membranes when no protein of interest is synthesized in situ. Therefore, adsorption measurements carried out under those conditions are characteristic of the interactions between the IIMPs and the membrane only.

To demonstrate the specificity of IIMPs to the lipid composition of the membranes, we used two membrane proteins with well-known and different lipid selectivity and sensitivity. Alpha-hemolysin (AH) is a pore-forming protein that integrates into membranes made of lipids found in higher organisms like human cells, such as phosphatidylcholine (PC). MscL, a mechano-sensitive channel from E. coli, integrates into membranes made of lipids (ECL) found in bacteria. We showed that AH and MscL integrate exclusively into membranes made of their specific lipids. When hybrid membranes mixing PC and ECL lipids were made, we observed that both AH and MscL can integrate into the membranes at different degrees depending on the fraction of each lipid in the membrane. This experiment showed that SCs with hybrid membranes made of lipids from different biological kingdoms can be engineered.

To determine whether the TXTL-QCMD approach enables the sensing of membrane-based dynamical patterns, we assayed the E. coli Min system that uses the inner membrane to position the cell division machinery via pole-to-pole dynamical oscillations. The MinCDE system in E. coli, composed of the protein MinC, MinD, and MinE, oscillates from pole to pole to precisely center the FtsZ cell division ring. We showed that TXTL-QCMD reconstitutes the oscillations of the MinCDE system. We characterized the lipid sensitivity of MinCDE and observed that PG (phosphatidylglycerol) and PE (phosphatidylethanolamine), both present in E. coli membrane, are essential for oscillations. The amplitude of the oscillations is amplified when two-dimensional crowding is emulated by simply adding neutral polymers at the membrane.

In the last experiment, we used TXTL-QCMD to decipher the membrane biochemistry of the recently discovered Zorya anti-phage system that is unamenable to labeling in vivo. We discovered that ZorA and ZorB integrate within the lipids found at the poles of bacteria while ZorE diffuses freely on non-polar membrane lipids.

These efforts establish the potential of TXTL-QCMD to broadly characterize the large diversity of IIMPs. The TXTL-QCMD approach is fast, non-disruptive, and reproducible. It enables assaying single or concurrently in-situ synthesized IIMPs on membranes with arbitrarily complex lipid compositions on physical scales that tolerate the formation of large dynamical patterns. We anticipate that it could be useful for the bottom-up engineering of SCs.

In addition to research, one postdoc and two graduate students were trained during the project, and two REU students (Research Experience for Undergraduates) were hosted during summers. The results of the research were disseminated through several talks given at domestic and international conferences, and several publications.

abstractText:
Demand for wireless data services will continue to rise rapidly in the foreseeable future.  The goal of this project is to develop new advanced solutions for wireless access networks with the objectives of increasing network throughput and maximizing overall network utilities.  Long-serving model-based solutions are facing severe limitations due to delays in tracking the ever-changing radio and network environment as well as measurement inaccuracies.  The main novelty of this project is to bring new tools based on artificial neural networks (ANN) to meet those challenges.  In particular, this project will investigate when, how, and why ANN-based learning techniques can be applied to a wide range of wireless networking problems with realistic constraints.  This project will pursue transformative solutions that aim to benefit academia and industry alike.  
 
Specifically, this project will marry supervised and unsupervised learning techniques with time-tested models of physical resources, channels, traffic, and network utilities.  An important task is to exploit commonalities of ANN-based solutions for a number of subproblems to develop a set of principled, holistic solutions for the overall wireless networking problem, seeking solutions that are scalable, computationally efficient, and highly adaptive.  Pertinent learnability and complexity theories backing the solutions will also be developed, in order to offer generalizable design principles. The ANN-based solutions developed are expected to be a major building block of next generation wireless access networks with associated economic benefits.

projectOutComesReport:
Wireless communication networks are the backbone of our connected society. As demands on these networks continue to grow—driven by applications such as 5G, autonomous systems, and the Internet of Things—new approaches are needed to efficiently allocate limited spectrum resources and manage interference among devices. This project explored how modern advances in machine learning (ML) and optimization can be used to design faster, smarter, and more adaptive wireless networks.

Intellectual Merit
Over the course of the award, the research team made several advances at the intersection of machine learning, mathematical optimization, and wireless communications.

  1. Comprehensive Foundations.The PI is part of the team that organized a special issue of the IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications on “Advanced Optimization Theory and Algorithms for Next Generation Wireless Communication Networks.” As part of this effort, they authored a comprehensive survey summarizing how optimization and ML methods are transforming wireless system design. The survey not only synthesized state-of-the-art results but also highlighted open challenges and research opportunities, helping to guide the broader community.

  2. New Algorithms for Wireless Optimization. The project developed a suite of machine learning–based methods to address problems that combine both discrete choices (such as which antennas or users to select) and continuous decisions (such as power allocation). These problems are notoriously difficult to solve with traditional techniques. The team proposed:

    • A Transformer-based two-stage approach for user scheduling and beamforming, which drastically reduces computational time compared to existing heuristics.

    • A “learning to beamform” framework for massive MIMO networks, which generalizes across heterogeneous deployments and achieves high performance with lower runtime.

    • Graph neural network–augmented branch-and-bound algorithms that accelerate the solution of mixed-integer problems by an order of magnitude, while still guaranteeing near-optimal solutions.

  3. Theoretical Understanding of ML for Wireless. Beyond algorithms, the project contributed theoretical insights into how supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised learning methods perform in interference management tasks. The findings showed when each approach is reliable, why unsupervised training may fail in certain cases, and how hybrid semi-supervised methods can combine the strengths of both paradigms. These results provided clarity to a rapidly growing research area and established principles for designing ML-based wireless models.

  4. Dynamic and Data-Driven Wireless Design. Recognizing that wireless environments are constantly changing, the team developed a continual learning framework that allows ML models to adapt to new interference conditions without forgetting previously learned knowledge. This bilevel optimization–based design ensures fairness across scenarios and was successfully demonstrated for both power control and beamforming tasks. In addition, the team advanced the field of spectrum cartography by developing new ML techniques to reconstruct high-resolution radio maps from sparse measurements. Their emitter-disaggregation approach improves accuracy, robustness to noise, and scalability, and was validated on real-world datasets.

Broader Impacts
This project has produced both fundamental knowledge and practical tools with lasting impact. The algorithms and theoretical results advance the scientific understanding of how ML and optimization can be applied to nonconvex, interference-limited wireless networks. At the same time, they offer practical solutions for real-world problems such as resource allocation, antenna selection, and spectrum monitoring. These contributions support the development of next-generation communication technologies that will benefit industries, government agencies, and the public at large.

Beyond research, the project helped train graduate students at the intersection of machine learning, optimization, and wireless communications. The project also generated open-access publications, including survey and tutorial papers, which serve as valuable resources for the broader research community.

In summary, this project demonstrated how artificial intelligence can be harnessed to design wireless systems that are more efficient, adaptive, and scalable. By bridging theory and practice, it contributed to both the intellectual foundations and the technological advances needed to build the wireless networks of the future.

abstractText:
What makes COVID-19 spread rapidly in some places, yet slowly in others? How should society lessen social distancing while limiting an increase in infections? To answer these questions, this Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project seeks to understand how patterns of interpersonal interaction (“structure”) in social contact networks affect disease spread in a population. The researchers will simulate a disease spreading through a variety of social contact networks, and use machine learning to relate each network’s structure to the number and timing of new infections. By limiting structures related to increased disease, societies may be able to reopen other parts of their economies while still curbing overall disease spread. The researchers will produce an interactive web application for the public and decision-makers to visualize trade-offs between reducing disease and maintaining social cohesion. This research will support the professional development of an early career scientist.

This research aims to determine the inherent risk of SARS-CoV-2 spread based on contact network structure. The researchers will use machine learning to 1) identify network structures that influence disease spread and 2) predict disease spread on empirical contact networks. Important network structures will serve as targets for simulated disease mitigation interventions (e.g. reducing structures that increase levels of disease or increasing structures that reduce disease levels). Finally, the researchers will investigate whether future outbreaks of COVID-19 or other diseases could be alleviated through optimizing social contact networks ahead of time. The outcomes of this research will inform and facilitate quick, efficient interventions to reduce the social and economic costs of COVID-19. This research will develop a general framework for relating disease to network structure. Thus, results can be generalized beyond the current pandemic, serving to further our understanding of potential future waves of COVID-19, as well as other directly-transmitted diseases in humans, livestock, and wildlife.

This RAPID award is made by the Ecology and Evolution of Infectious Diseases Program in the Division of Environmental Biology, using funds from the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act

projectOutComesReport:
This grant for rapid response research (RAPID) sought to explore the role of contact network structure on the spread of COVID-19 and similarly transmitted pathogens. Over the course of this funding, Drs. Craft, Michalska-Smith, and Enns have considered the relationship between the patterns of interpersonal interaction (that is, "contact network structure") and the dynamics of disease spread through a population at two levels.

First, they considered variables that determine contact network structure in empirical populations, such as age- and household size distributions, individual differences in behavior, for instance as relates to risk-tolerance, and potential context-specific differences in interaction patterns, for instance comparing workplace interactions to those at school or within a household. This research culminated in both a peer-reviewed published manuscript and a publicly accessible online application for both education and experimental use, as well as presentation of these results at a national academic conference.

One major finding of this work was the importance of community-wide action in limiting disease spread. Because modern societies are highly interconnected, there are many avenues for a pathogen to spread to those individuals most at risk of adverse outcomes. As a consequence, we found that when prevention measures are only undertaken by these vulnerable individuals, there was limited effect on overall disease spread. In contrast, if household members also participated, we saw dramatic reductions in disease and mortality. This work has clear implications for public health recommendations and policies, which most often focus on individuals themselves, rather than their ability to spread the disease to others.

Second, they looked at the effect of individuals moving between populations (cities, for instance) on the disease dynamics in each of the populations involved. This work, conducted at a general level that allows application to a variety of disease systems, including those in both livestock and wildlife, culminated in a peer-reviewed academic publication and presentation at a national academic conference.

In brief, the researchers found that the movement of individuals can have dramatic effects on the dynamics of disease, for instance stabilizing prevalence in a population where it was once fluctuating, or introducing fluctuations where the infected proportion of a population was relatively constant. The key determiner of the direction of this change was the dynamics of disease in the population from which the migrants were emigrating from.

Finally, they considered specific measures of network structure at the level of a whole population, including, for instance, the degree of clustering (are your friends also friends with each other?) and the distribution of interactions across individuals (does everyone have about the same number of contacts, or do a small subset have many while most people have few?). This research is ongoing, but has produced one manuscript in preparation for publication so far, as well as presentation of preliminary results at a national academic conference.

This award provides funding for two small regional conferences that will continue to rotate among the three host institutions: Iowa State University, the University of Minnesota, and the University of Wisconsin. These conferences promote a broad view of commutative algebra, inspiring conversations, and collaborations between different areas of algebra. This is a continuation of a conference series, with two meetings each at Minnesota and Wisconsin between 2015 and 2017. After a brief hiatus, Iowa State University will join the rotation, hosting the conference in 2020 before the event returns to Minnesota in 2021. 
 
Commutative algebra  is filled with connections to other areas, including: algebraic geometry, algebraic topology, combinatorics, number theory, applied algebra, representation theory, computational algebra, and more.  The conference series supported by this award promotes a broad view of commutative algebra, helping connect it with the research environments in the mathematics departments involved.
Information about the conference will be found at http://www-users.math.umn.edu/~cberkesc/CA/CA.html

This project hosts small regional conferences that rotate among the three host institutions: Iowa State University, the University of Minnesota, and the University of Wisconsin. These conferences promote a broad view of commutative algebra, inspiring conversations, and collaborations between different areas of algebra. 

The smaller size of these conferences enables us to focus invitations on plenary speakers who are both doing cutting-edge research and have a record of excellent exposition. This promotes the training and education of graduate students and postdocs who attend and interact with these speakers.  In addition, this advances discovery, as graduate students, postdocs, and junior faculty  learn about exciting new work  in commutative algebra.

This meeting also supports the development of research programs for the organizers (Berkesch, Erman, McCullough) and their graduate students and postdocs, through the development of a robust research community and through interactions with the plenary speakers and the local researchers at our institutions.

The organizers are committed to highlighting the work of women researchers via our plenary speakers. To further broaden the participation of underrepresented groups, they also recruit and support graduate students and postdocs from underrepresented groups--including students interested in commutative algebra but working at an outside institution.

The specific talks under this award were given by Patricia Klein, Monica Lewis, Matthew Mastoeni, Victor Reiner, and Botong Wang in 2021 and Hang (Amy) Huang, Janet Page, Michael Perlman, Mahrud Sayrafi, and Mark Walker in 2023.

This Research Experiences for Teachers (RET) in Engineering Site program is hosted by the National Nanotechnology Coordinated Infrastructure (NNCI) with the lead at Georgia Institute of Technology and partners at the University of Minnesota; University of Nebraska, Lincoln; and Northwestern University. This program, entitled "RET Site: Collaborative Research: Research Experiences for Teachers across the National Nanotechnology Coordinated Infrastructure", will provide a total of 60 (20 per year for 3 years), in-service, high school and community college faculty (CCF) within commuting distance of the NNCI university site an opportunity to engage in high-quality, nanoscale science and engineering (NSE) hands-on research in state-of-the-art nanotechnology facilities at four NNCI sites for 6 weeks during the summer with 1 week of follow-up activities throughout the year. The objectives of this program are to grow a multi-site cohort of educators with research experiences that reflect broad educational, industrial, and societal NSE activities and link them with the Teaching Nano and Emerging Technologies Network (https://www.nano.gov/TeacherNetwork); build and disseminate a library of NSE educational materials; highlight the work of NNCI cohort by attending the National Science Teachers Association (NSTA) conference; and encourage RETs to present at professional society meetings.

Educators will complete a hands-on research project in NSE during the summer with continuing support during the academic year. The RET projects will cover a wide range of topics spanning the breadth of NSE. With support from faculty, mentors, and RET coordinators, the RETs will develop curriculum materials to bring their NSE research back to their classrooms. During the academic year, faculty and mentors will visit the RET classrooms to assist with the implementation and further development of the curriculum modules. Participating in the NNCI RET program will help teachers and CCF motivate their students to explore STEM and NSE fields that will provide them with satisfying and life long careers in the 21st century economy. This RET program spans four NNCI sites allowing participants access to a wider variety of NSE research than would be available at a single-site, and exposing participants to the NSE needs of industry and related career opportunities across the nation. Webinars will be held across all participating NNCI sites to enable teachers to learn about NSE industries and careers as well as to discuss their modules. The RET program will also allow networking opportunities from the widest range of teacher backgrounds through participation in on-line presentations and webinars, a LinkedIn group, at the yearly NSTA conference, and at professional society conferences.

projectOutComesReport:
The Research Experiences for Teachers Across the National Nanotechnology Coordinated Infrastructure (NNCI) program focuses on nanoscale science and engineering. Four universities from across the NNCI took part in the program: the Georgia Institute of Technology, the University of Minnesota, the University of Nebraska – Lincoln, and Northwestern University. These four institutions supported secondary and community college educators for a series of six-week summer research experiences with follow-up support during the school semesters. The networked approach for this program allowed the participating educators to take part in a wider array of NSE research opportunities and interactions than would have been possible through a single university. The follow outcomes were achieved as part of the University of Minnesota collaborative effort.

Over the summers of 2021-2023, a total of twelve high-school teachers from the Twin Cities area were hosted at the University of Minnesota and participated in projects aimed at enhancing their skills in teaching concepts in the field of nanoscale science and engineering to high-school students. The participant teachers were mentored by university researchers and received hands-on training in laboratory procedures and techniques. The teachers were able to build connections with colleagues at the other collaborating universities to share knowledge across the multi-site cohort and compare lesson plan topics. Teachers were also able to develop an understanding of the commercial relevance of nanoscale science and engineering topics through interactions with industry representatives. These interactions helped to connect the teachers to companies that locally employ talent trained in micro- and nanotechnology, while also giving them a national perspective on possible job opportunities for their students. Some of the educators also received valuable experiences through participation in the National Science Teaching Association (NSTA) conference, where they were able to interact with a wider range of peers to share ideas and techniques in the field of science education.

A particularly important outcome of the program was the development of lesson plans on nanoscale science and engineering. These plans not only could be used in the individual teachers’ classrooms, but have also been made available on a public-facing website. The lesson plans were carefully developed and made available to peers and provided to students so that feedback and input could be obtained before finalization. The completed lesson plans have been added to the K-16 Curriculum Materials database on the NNCI website, and are also planned to be included on other platforms as well. Lesson videos were also produced that can be posted on public websites. These materials have the impact of widening the scope of nanoscale science and engineering education, allowing more students to understand this important technology, and enabling a wider range of teachers to access these learning resources.

Overall, the educators in this program came away better equipped to effectively teach and mentor students in the field of nanotechnology. The teachers also achieved improvements in presenting research results and in applying research literature concepts to their own work. The enhanced teaching skills developed as part of this program are important steps to better equip the next generation of scientists and engineers.
